title: Institutionalized expertise and strategic deferral: explaining Japan’s delayed response to declining fertility
authors: Gayoung Kaei Choi
abstract: Abstract This article explains Japan’s delayed policy response to declining fertility by examining how institutionalized expertise shaped population governance in the post-war period. Existing studies emphasize weak problem recognition, taboos surrounding state-led population policy, and agenda-setting dynamics, but they rarely examine how these factors interacted within institutional settings. To address this gap, the article develops an analytical framework linking institutions, ideas, and behaviour that clarifies how expert interpretations translated into policy action within Japan’s population policy advisory system. Applying this framework, the analysis demonstrates that the advisory system functioned as an institutional arena in which expert interpretations were produced, authorized, and disseminated, whilst political accountability conditioned their translation into policy action. Within this setting, experts engaged actively, whereas government actors responded through a recurrent pattern of strategic deferral. These asymmetric responses reflected divergent interpretations of demographic conditions and appropriate policy action. This interaction produced what the article terms restrained intervention: indirect regulation, authorized shelving, and issue displacement. The article makes two contributions. Substantively, it explains why Japan repeatedly produced restrained intervention despite sustained fertility decline. Analytically, it argues that institutionalized expertise does not necessarily accelerate policy change; under conditions of political accountability, it can instead structure and legitimate deferral. Demographic concerns are channelled through procedurally appropriate consultation and reframed in politically acceptable terms, thereby enabling governments to defer explicit state-led intervention. This perspective shifts comparative inquiry from why governments fail to act to how policy inaction is institutionally produced and sustained.

title: When Silence Must Be Proven: The Burden of Abstention in Artificial Intelligence
authors: Teodor Minchev
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Description This work introduces accountable abstention as a missing and necessary primitive in the governance of artificial intelligence systems. Building on prior research on question-first cognition, cognitive permission, legitimacy gating, and governed silence, the paper argues that the ability of an AI system to justify and evidence its non-participation is as critical as its ability to reason correctly. Contemporary AI governance frameworks increasingly recognize that illegitimate cognition—reasoning without sufficient epistemic grounding, authority, or consequence awareness—is a dominant risk. However, silence and refusal are typically treated as terminal safety outcomes rather than accountable epistemic acts. This work challenges that assumption. We argue that systems which cannot demonstrate that they were capable of reasoning, evaluated legitimacy, and intentionally refrained from cognition under epistemic pressure are structurally unsafe, regardless of output correctness or downstream safety controls. Silence without accountability provides no epistemic assurance and cannot support regulatory, institutional, or audit requirements in high-stakes domains. The paper formalizes the Burden of Abstention: the requirement that intelligent systems be able to prove that non-participation was possible, intentional, and structurally enforced prior to reasoning activation. It reframes abstention not as the absence of cognition, but as an active, governed epistemic act subject to accountability without reintroducing authority simulation. This work is conceptual and architectural rather than algorithmic. It proposes no implementations or training methods. Its contribution lies in extending AI governance from legitimacy of reasoning to responsibility for restraint, establishing accountable non-action as a first-class constraint for intelligent systems operating in regulated and high-consequence environments.

title: ContractRL: Shielded Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Auditable Tool-Call Repair
authors: Miaobo Hu; Shuhao Hu; Xiaobo Guo; Xin Wang; Bokun Wang; Yina Sa; Daren Zha
abstract: Structured tool calls often fail after only a small number of fields violate a schema or an execution contract. Regenerating the complete object enlarges the action surface and makes repeated repair difficult to audit. We introduce ContractRL, a contract-constrained sequential repair protocol that models verifier-guided JSON repair as a bounded decision process. At each step the policy observes the candidate, typed verifier feedback, JSON Pointer, immutable repair history, and remaining budget; a contract-derived action mask filters malformed or prohibited RFC-6902 operations before a deterministic validator performs the transition. We specify a contract-constrained group-relative objective for patch, retry, and abstention decisions while keeping canonical targets and semantic labels outside the online state until trace freeze. Under identical verifier information, ContractRL attains 0.9362 semantic success with 34.4 generated tokens, compared with 0.9076 and 44.9 tokens for Patch-SFT and 0.9148 and 137.2 tokens for full regeneration over 192 cases per seed and five seeds. Policy optimization improves semantic success from 0.9186 for supervised ContractRL to 0.9375. A separate three-seed paired evaluation against Patch-SFT yields a semantic difference of +0.0396 (95% CI $[+0.0137,+0.0662], p=0.0039$). Feedback, action-mask, budget, and schema-shift analyses connect these gains to localized correction, while adversarial and multi-turn evaluations characterize the remaining failure modes.

title: MultiRetNet: A Multimodal Vision Model and Deferral System for Staging Diabetic Retinopathy
authors: She, Jeannie; Katie Spivakovsky
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of preventable blindness, affecting over 100 million people worldwide. In the United States, individuals from lower-income communities face a higher risk of progressing to advanced stages before diagnosis, largely due to limited access to screening. Comorbid conditions further accelerate disease progression. We propose MultiRetNet, a novel pipeline combining retinal imaging, socioeconomic factors, and comorbidity profiles to improve DR staging accuracy, integrated with a clinical deferral system for a clinical human-in-the-loop implementation. We experiment with three multimodal fusion methods and identify fusion through a fully connected layer as the most versatile methodology. We synthesize adversarial, low-quality images and use contrastive learning to train the deferral system, guiding the model to identify out-of-distribution samples that warrant clinician review. By maintaining diagnostic accuracy on suboptimal images and integrating critical health data, our system can improve early detection, particularly in underserved populations where advanced DR is often first identified. This approach may reduce healthcare costs, increase early detection rates, and address disparities in access to care, promoting healthcare equity.

title: OpenMTB-Audit: Exposing Over-Refusal and Clinical Expert Perspectives in LLM-Based Molecular Tumor Board Safety Evaluation
authors: Negin Ashrafi; Jia Luo; Stacey M. Frumm; Roxana Daneshjou
abstract: Molecular tumor boards integrate genomic findings, clinical context, and therapeutic evidence to support precision oncology. As AI enters this workflow, a key safety challenge is distinguishing truly unsupported recommendations from evidence-supported options that still require oncologist review because of incomplete information, poor ECOG performance status, or other clinical caveats. We introduce OpenMTB-Audit, an open-source benchmark of 500 synthetic non-small cell lung cancer cases spanning five adversarial error categories and four safety labels: Supported, Partially Supported, Unsupported, and Insufficient Information. Across eight large language model configurations, we identify pervasive over-refusal: all LLM configurations failed to retain the Partially Supported label in 83.3-100% of true Partially Supported cases, achieving high aggregate safety scores through label collapse rather than clinically calibrated reasoning. To address this limitation, we developed MTB-AuditAgent, a deterministic seven-module framework separating evidence verification, missing-information detection, safety classification, and abstention. It reduces over-refusal to 6.7% and achieves 91.2% accuracy (95% CI: 88.6-93.6%). A two-oncologist annotation study found disagreement concentrated at the boundary between information sufficiency and treatment optimization, underscoring the need to preserve clinically meaningful distinctions.

title: Learned Class-Conditional Signal- Quality Deferral for Selective rPPG- Based Atrial Fibrillation Screening
authors: Shahnawaz Khan
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Selective-prediction methodology for contactless atrial- fibrillation (AF) screening from remote-photoplethysmography (rPPG) signals derived from face video. Introduces Learned Class-Conditional Signal-Quality Deferral (LW-CCSD), a post-hoc model-agnostic deferral policy that learns per-predicted-class weights combining model confidence with spectral signal-to-noise ratio, subject to a configurable per-class recall floor. On a 45,064-segment synthetic-rPPG benchmark derived from the PhysioNet/CinC 2017 AF Challenge, LW-CCSD achieves a tunable Pareto frontier between selective accuracy and AF-recall safety (+4.1 percent AURC at essentially zero AF-recall cost, scaling to +15.6 percent AURC at 8 percentage-point AF cost). A Clopper- Pearson conformal extension provides finite-sample distribution- free coverage guarantees with essentially zero operational penalty (identical operating point at 90 percent confidence; 0.6 percent relative AURC cost at 95 percent confidence). LW-CCSD applied to a single-pass deterministic classifier achieves better selective performance than a five-model deep ensemble without LW-CCSD, suggesting the method can substitute for compute-expensive ensembling in deployed clinical screens. Cross-UQ replication (deterministic, MC Dropout, deep ensembles) and orthogonal SNR-tertile and HR-tertile stratifications confirm the cross-regime mechanism. Repository includes the full reproducibility chain: pipeline, configurations, trained checkpoints, per-method evaluation artefacts, paper LaTeX and HTML sources, and figure generation scripts.

title: Ethical Blood Donor Deferral in a Tertiary Hospital of North India
authors: Kusam Thakur; Rajni Bassi; Kanchan Bhardwaj
venue: Journal of Punjab Academy of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology
abstract: Pre donation blood donor screening is done for the safety of the donor and recipient. Individuals disqualified from donating blood are known as “deferred” donors. Donor deferral might appear as discrimination and violation of a human right. Deferring prospective donors often leaves them with negative feelings about themselves as well as the blood donation process. Additionally these donors are less likely to return for blood donation in future. So causes of the pre-blood donation deferral need to be studied systematically to improve the donation rate. Retrospective observational study was done for whole blood donations over a period from April 2016 to December 2016. Out of 16298 blood donors who came to donate blood, 15783 (96.84%) were males and 515 (03.16%) were females. Total 1766 (10.83%) blood donors were deferred, out of which 1706 (96.6%) were temporary deferrals and 60 (3.4%) were permanently deferred. Overall more males (1413) were deferred than females (353) but females had higher deferral rate (68.5%) than males (8.9%). Effective measures need to be initiated to address the issue of lost donors due to temporary deferrals which can be reduced by providing detailed information and educating the donors & camp organizer by blood bank staff. Donors with permanent deferrals should be counseled, notified and referred to specialists for further treatment.

title: Governance-Aware Human-in-the-Loop AI for Structuring Longitudinal Autism Intervention Evidence and Generating Evidence-Linked Reports: Development and Component Evaluation Study
authors: Ambar Nath Saha; Debashis Patra
abstract: Longitudinal autism intervention review requires specialists to combine observations from caregivers, teachers, and intervention staff across settings and time. We developed a governance-aware human-in-the-loop application that uses AI to organize evidence while keeping intervention decisions with professionals. The system preserves original observations, proposes structured records with Qwen 2.5 7B, requires professional verification or correction before analytics, checks evidence adequacy, supports abstention, and produces traceable reports. Evaluation used archival ASDBank data from 11 children, 85 sessions, and 9,018 behavioral episodes. Two experienced autism specialists created the reference standard, followed by a final-codebook compliance audit. Qwen 2.5 7B achieved 41.3% merged categorical agreement on the 330-segment main batch and remained the strongest evaluated generator. The offline MARS selector returned records for 80.3% of segments but showed no clear field-level advantage over the strongest reviewable generator. A historical generative-reporting experiment failed its full governance contract (0/11), motivating deterministic operational reporting. Final controlled end-to-end testing passed all predefined governance scenarios (77/77 API tests and 9/9 UI scenarios). These findings support a practical architecture in which AI assists evidence organization, while professional review, abstention, provenance, and deterministic controls protect the longitudinal workflow.

title: Pattern of Blood Donor Deferral in a Blood Establishment in Lagos
authors: AK Orolu; BI Osikomaiya; BT Bello; AD Samuel; OG Animashaun
abstract: BACKGROUND: Donor deferrals serve a critical safety function in transfusion, yet high deferral rates may negatively impact blood supply and future donor return. Understanding the epidemiology and reasons for deferral can guide targeted interventions and policy adjustments. AIM: To determine the rate, pattern, and factors associated with pre-donation deferral among voluntary blood donors at the Lagos State Blood Transfusion Services (LSBTS) donation center. METHODS: A retrospective cross-sectional review of donor records was conducted over 12 months (January to December 2019) at LSBTS. Data were extracted from donation and deferral registers on donor demographics, type, and causes of deferral. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software version 28.0. Chi-square tests assessed associations between categorical variables, and t-tests compared continuous variables. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for selected associations. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. RESULTS: Of 5,427 prospective donors, 854 (15.7%) were deferred. Deferral rates varied significantly across age groups; P < 0.001. Temporary deferrals accounted for 98.0% of all deferrals, with low hemoglobin being the leading cause (46.3%). In multivariable logistic regression, female donors remained independently associated with donor deferral (adjusted OR [AOR] 5.84, 95% CI: 4.98-6.86; P < 0.001), while first-time donors had higher odds of deferral than repeat donors (AOR 1.34, 95% CI: 1.15-1.56; P < 0.001). CONCLUSION: To promote donor retention and maintain an adequate and safe blood supply, blood services should prioritize pre-donation education, adopt gender-sensitive eligibility guidelines, and implement policy updates informed by local population characteristics.

title: Gender‐neutral donor deferral policies: experience in Argentina implementing individual risk‐assessment policies
authors: Sebastián Blanco; Luis Carrizo; Rolando Walter Moyano; Arnaldo Pedro Mangeaud; Sandra Verónica Gallego
abstract: BACKGROUND: In Argentina, with the aim of moving to a safe supportive and inclusive National Blood System, in September 2015 the Ministry of Health stipulated that eligibility criteria for blood donation should only take into account the so-called 'risk practices', focusing on a 'gender-neutral' policy. The aim of this study is to demonstrate the impact of such regulation on the prevalence of STI in the population of blood donors in Argentina, through the analysis of the scientific evidence obtained from 174 074 donors from a large central region of the country, focused on a regional Blood Bank for a 6-year period (pre- and post-entry into force of the regulations). MATERIALS AND METHODS: To analyse the evolution of prevalence rates of STI, two periods of 3 years each were evaluated: The first period (P1) lasted from 16 September 2012 to 15 September 2015 (prior to the entry into force of the law) and the second one (P2) from 16 September 2015 to 15 September 2018 (after the entry into force of the law). RESULTS: A total of 82 838 subjects were enrolled in P1 and 91 236 in P2. The results show a significantly lower prevalence of HCV (P = 0·029), HBV (P = 0·028) and syphilis (P = 0·001) in P2, while no difference was observed for HIV infection (P = 0·60). CONCLUSION: This study evidenced that the implementation of a 'gender-neutral' policy based on individual risk-assessment deferral criteria maintained the safety of blood supply and decreased the prevalence of STI among blood donors.

title: Knowing when not to carve: calibrated abstention for fragmented JPEG and PNG recovery
authors: Yaw Osei Adjei; Benjamin Tei Partey; Augustine Osei-Wusu; Eric Okpoti
abstract: This is a retrospective registration. The hypotheses and analysis plan were written and hashed on 8 October 2026 (02:00 UTC), before any evaluation image was generated. They were not lodged with a public registry at that time, although the plan itself called for registration. This registration is made after all analyses were run and after the manuscript was drafted. The time evidence for the plan is the SHA-256 hashes in the attached file `frozen-config-hashes.txt`: the hypotheses and plan (8 October 2026, 02:00 UTC), the test split (03:38 UTC) and the triage configuration (05:55 UTC). We therefore describe the analysis as pre-specified and hash-frozen, and we do not describe it as pre-registered. Summary of the study. A carver for baseline sequential JPEG and PNG files attaches a calibrated confidence to each reconstructed object. A triage labels each object Positive, Recovery or Irrecoverable. We evaluate it on synthetic fragmented disk images with ground truth. Outcome in one sentence. The pre-specified recovery criterion (H1) was not met, and neither primary hypothesis H2 nor H3 was supported as pre-specified.

title: BioGemma-Guard: Enhancing Calibrated Abstention in Clinical LLMs through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)
authors: Narendra Bayutama Wibisono
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) deployed in clinical settings face a critical safety deficit: they tend to generate confident-sounding diagnoses even when presented with insufficient or ambiguous patient data—a failure mode known as overconfident hallucination. In high-stakes environments such as emergency triage, such fabricated certainty can lead to misdiagnosis, delayed treatment, or inappropriate clinical escalation. We introduce BioGemma-Guard, a medical triage assistant built upon Google's Gemma-2-2B instruction-tuned model and aligned using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a custom four-tier clinical reward function. Our reward architecture assigns differential signals for diagnostic accuracy (+2.0), honest abstention on ambiguous inputs (+0.8), structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning (+0.2), and applies a severe penalty for hallucinated diagnoses on insufficient data (−3.0). We train BioGemma-Guard using parameter-efficient Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on a curated paired dataset of 200 clinical cases, each presented in both a clear and a noisy variant, enabling the model to learn both diagnostic precision and principled uncertainty. Evaluation via a two-stage LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline—first categorical classification (LLaMA-3.3-70B), then granular quantitative scoring (LLaMA-4-Scout-17B-16E)—reveals that while core medical knowledge is fully preserved (Clinical Faithfulness: 7.96 → 7.98; Differential Quality: 6.84 → 6.84), Chain-of-Thought Discipline improves significantly from 7.68 to 8.24 (Δ = +0.56), with standard deviation decreasing from 2.14 to 1.39. Notably, GRPO training eliminates the lowest-quality reasoning traces entirely (score=2 cases: 3 → 0) and increases the proportion of high-discipline responses (score ≥ 9) from 66% to 74%. Softmax confidence analysis reveals that both models converge on approximately 66.9% transition probability when facing high-entropy clinical inputs, indicating appropriately calibrated uncertainty rather than reckless guessing. BioGemma-Guard thus demonstrates that reinforcement learning alignment can enhance the structural discipline of clinical reasoning without degrading medical knowledge—a prerequisite for trustworthy AI deployment in healthcare. Keywords: Medical AI, Large Language Models, Calibrated Abstention, GRPO, Reinforcement Learning, Chain-of-Thought Reasoning, Conformal Prediction, Clinical Triage, Hallucination Mitigation

title: Implementation of the Individual Risk Assessment and Changes to Deferral Periods Since 2020
authors: Todd Straus; Daniela Hermelin; Emily A. Coberly

title: Potential benefits of an alternative haemoglobin deferral strategy evaluated in seven countries
authors: Amber Meulenbeld; Claire E. Styles; Glen Shuttleworth; Supun Sudaraka Manathunga; Hans Van Remoortel; Lucile Malard; Tinus Brits; Ronél Swanevelder; José Antonio García‐Erce; Iris Garcia-martinez A; Surendra Karki; Marijke Welvaert; W. Alton Russell; Mikko Arvas; Katja van den Hurk; Mart Pothast; Mart P. Janssen
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: On-site donor deferral for low haemoglobin (Hb) levels poses significant challenges for blood establishments globally, leading to material wastage and consumption of valuable staff and donor time. Traditionally, donors are deferred based on a single visit's Hb measurement, without considering previous Hb levels and measurement variability. This study aims to quantify, in different settings, the potential impact of an alternative deferral algorithm based on historical mean Hb levels. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We retrospectively reassessed donor eligibility in 20,430,816 donations and deferrals in Australia, Belgium, Finland, France, the Netherlands, South Africa and the United States using an algorithm that considers a repeat donor eligible as long as their historical mean Hb is above the deferral threshold and deviations from the mean are consistent with anticipated measurement variability. We quantified the potential impact of the alternative algorithm by calculating the change in donations and deferrals. RESULTS: Across countries, the alternative algorithm may reduce low Hb deferrals between 30% and 70%. Additionally, in every country, a small proportion of current donors (~1%) donate who exhibit consistent low Hb levels. Balancing new deferrals and donations, the estimated net increase in donations across countries ranges between 0.7% and 3.3%. CONCLUSION: The alternative deferral algorithm based on mean Hb levels is a first step towards a more comprehensive assessment of Hb levels to determine donor eligibility. Further research is needed to refine the algorithm, to determine its long-term impact, to improve the model with information related to iron stores and recovery and to address the impact on donor safety.

title: Neural Bayesian Sequential Routing
authors: Yongchao Huang
abstract: Human decision-making is sequential and uncertainty-aware, yet standard neural networks often rely on static, dense forward computation with limited visibility into evidence acquisition, uncertainty evolution, or when computation should stop. We introduce \textbf{Neural Bayesian Sequential Routing (NBSR)}, a framework that models neural inference as active evidence accumulation over a hierarchical Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Within a Dirichlet--Categorical conjugate framework, neural experts query a persistent global knowledge oracle to extract positive evidence vectors, which act as pseudo-counts and update a Dirichlet belief state by exact conjugate addition. Coupled with a Gumbel-Softmax Straight-Through estimator, this update enables hard, path-dependent routing while preserving surrogate gradients for end-to-end training. The resulting Dirichlet precision and entropy provide mechanisms for uncertainty quantification, entropy-based early exiting, OOD abstention, and cost-aware evidence acquisition. We prove that, under strictly positive evidence extraction, total Dirichlet precision increases monotonically along any valid trajectory and marginal predictive variance is bounded, formalizing sequential ``hypothesis sharpening''; under idealized capacity and optimization assumptions, the terminal Dirichlet expectation recovers the Bayes-optimal conditional distribution. Empirical evaluations across visual categorization, structured medical diagnosis, language modeling, partially observable control, and cost-aware Bayesian experimental design show that NBSR achieves competitive predictive performance while providing transparent routing traces, path-dependent evidence attribution, uncertainty-aware decision control, and resource-rational inference. Overall, NBSR offers a mathematically grounded framework for interpretable, modular, and resource-rational agentic AI.

title: Analysis of reasons for blood donor deferral in student population of Vojvodina
authors: Neda Kocic; Nevenka Bujandrić; Milomir Bezanovic; Milana Beronja
abstract: Introduction. The supply of blood from healthy blood donors (BD) is essential for safe blood transfusions. As students play an important role in providing adequate blood supplies, this study analyzes the frequency and reasons for blood donor deferral among the student population of Vojvodina, with the intention of reducing the rate of deferral and improving re-entry. Material and Methods. A retrospective study examined blood donor deferral records of the University of Novi Sad students who donated blood at the Blood Transfusion Institute of Vojvodina, from January 1 to December 31, 2022. The deferrals have been categorized based on pre-donation deferral causes, the blood donor deferral period, in relevance to the safety of both the blood donor and the recipient. Results. Of 867 students in total, 121 (13.9%) were deferred from donating blood. 72/121 (59.5%) of them were female, 49/121 (11.3%) were male, and 99/121 (81.8%) were regular blood donors. Temporary deferrals of less than 3 months were recorded for 98/121 (80.99%) students, while deferrals for 6 months were applicable to 19/121 (15.7%), with 4/121 (3.3%) experiencing permanent deferrals. The number of blood donors deferred due to safety reasons of the very donors was 85/121 (70.2%). The most common reasons were low hemoglobin level 17/121 (14.1%), medication deferral (pain-killers, antihista?mines, antibiotics) 17/121 (14.1%) and adverse reactions prior to blood donation 15/121 (12.3%). Conclusion. Educating blood donors about high-risk behaviors, medication usage, screening for iron deficiency and hypertension could be the most important tool to reduce the rate of deferral and improve blood donor re-entry.

title: An Aumann-Shapley Approach to Allocate Capacity Deferral Benefit Among Distributed Energy Resources
authors: Shilpa Bindal; A. R. Abhyankar
abstract: High penetration of distributed energy resources provide power system planners with a practical substitute to high cost reinforcement plans. Locating DERs near load centers and optimizing their power dispatch, can reduce the utilization of power system assets resulting in the deferral of investments. To incentivize DERs to provide desired dispatch, it is essential to quantify their individual contribution towards capacity deferral benefits. This paper introduces an Aumann Shapley based allocation scheme that distrubutes deferral benefit among various DERs. The scheme is analytically validated against key fairness axioms desired by the DER stakeholders. A series of case studies on IEEE European distribution network are conducted to assess its fairness attributes. The results demonstrate that the proposed allocation scheme satisfies the desired fairness standards and also provides locational signal for future DER installations.

title: Selective Diabetic Retinopathy Screening with Accuracy-Weighted Deep Ensembles and Entropy-Guided Abstention
authors: Lin, Jophy
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), a microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading cause of preventable blindness, is projected to affect more than 130 million individuals worldwide by 2030. Early identification is essential to reduce irreversible vision loss, yet current diagnostic workflows rely on methods such as fundus photography and expert review, which remain costly and resource-intensive. This, combined with DR's asymptomatic nature, results in its underdiagnosis rate of approximately 25 percent. Although convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated strong performance in medical imaging tasks, limited interpretability and the absence of uncertainty quantification restrict clinical reliability. Therefore, in this study, a deep ensemble learning framework integrated with uncertainty estimation is introduced to improve robustness, transparency, and scalability in DR detection. The ensemble incorporates seven CNN architectures-ResNet-50, DenseNet-121, MobileNetV3 (Small and Large), and EfficientNet (B0, B2, B3)- whose outputs are fused through an accuracy-weighted majority voting strategy. A probability-weighted entropy metric quantifies prediction uncertainty, enabling low-confidence samples to be excluded or flagged for additional review. Training and validation on 35,000 EyePACS retinal fundus images produced an unfiltered accuracy of 93.70 percent (F1 = 0.9376). Uncertainty-filtering later was conducted to remove unconfident samples, resulting in maximum-accuracy of 99.44 percent (F1 = 0.9932). The framework shows that uncertainty-aware, accuracy-weighted ensembling improves reliability without hindering performance. With confidence-calibrated outputs and a tunable accuracy-coverage trade-off, it offers a generalizable paradigm for deploying trustworthy AI diagnostics in high-risk care.

title: Audit-Ready Patent Valuation: Evidence-Grounded Estimates with Calibrated Uncertainty and Abstention
authors: Amrutha Belakavady Sundaresha Moorthy
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In legal systems where monetary damages, licensing royalties, and market access are determined by IP value, patent valuation functions as an economic estimation exercise under legal constraint. Yet prevailing valuation approaches—such as Relief-from-Royalty, market comparables, and income-based models—typically obscure the evidentiary basis of their inputs and provide point estimates without calibrated measures of uncertainty. This opacity limits auditability, inflates disputes, and weakens trust in both expert testimony and automated valuation tools. This paper proposes an audit-ready patent valuation framework in which every numeric output is explicitly grounded in verifiable technical, product, and market evidence and accompanied by calibrated confidence measures. The framework integrates three components: (1) clause- and feature-level technical alignment evidence, (2) bibliometric, deployment, and market proxies with traceable provenance, and (3) a confidence and abstention policy that suppresses or withholds valuation outputs when evidentiary support falls below predefined thresholds. Rather than maximizing coverage, the model prioritizes reliability, reproducibility, and transparency. Using standards-driven patent disputes—including Optis v. Apple and IN244759 v. Xiaomi—we demonstrate how evidence-grounded valuation alters both absolute estimates and relative rankings compared to conventional approaches. We report calibration diagnostics, coverage–accuracy trade-offs, and abstention behavior under sparse or conflicting evidence. The paper contributes a valuation schema and evaluation protocol suitable for expert review, institutional audits, and policy-facing applications, reframing patent valuation as an evidence-constrained economic inference task with implications for judicial accuracy, licensing efficiency, and the governance of automated decision support.

title: Deferral of Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate Testing Before Contrast-Enhanced CT in Low-Risk Emergency Department Patients: Assessment of Safety and Impact on Throughput
authors: Gowthaman Gunabushanam; Daniella Asch; Janelle van Luling; Alexander Kuehne; Abedalrazaq O. AlKukhun; Lawrence H. Staib; Arjun K. Venkatesh; Jay K. Pahade
