title: Methodological Reflections on Researching Civil Society in Restrictive Environments
authors: Neya Global; Anna Neya Kazanskaia
abstract: Research on civil society in restrictive environments presents distinctive ethical, methodological, and security challenges. This article examines how scholars can conduct responsible, reflexive, and secure research amid surveillance, censorship, and repression. It focuses on three critical dimensions: ethics, digital security, and researcher positionality. Ethical practice extends beyond procedural consent to include contextual judgment, anonymization, and, at times, strategic abstention from fieldwork. Digital security is reframed as a methodological foundation, requiring encrypted tools, risk-aware design, and adaptive data management. Reflexivity regarding researcher identity and power dynamics is essential for equitable collaboration between local and foreign scholars. Through this synthesis, the article argues that ethical sensitivity and digital literacy are integral to methodological rigor. By embedding care and caution into research design, scholars can generate knowledge that advances understanding of civil society under pressure while prioritizing participant safety and agency.

title: STARLI | F111–F120 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · Collective Microrobotics, Fault Resilience and Trustworthy Autonomy Author: 33 | Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.2 | English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This collection presents ten prospective research-design monographs on distributed micro/nanorobotic collectives. Research Unit I (F111–F115) addresses limited communication, collaborative quantum sensing, consensus breakdown, dynamic task reassignment and joint human-machine authority. Research Unit II (F116–F120) examines misinformation propagation, graceful degradation, custody and mission integrity, cross-platform coordination and trustworthy autonomy. The ten studies propose falsifiable bench-scale experiments; none asserts demonstrated swarm intelligence, clinical efficacy or certified autonomous safety. The ten English working editions comprise 7,770 PDF pages in total: 300 prospective mathematical research plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study sections, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Gate proposes six annotated research dimensions: causal mechanism, measurable witness, blinded falsifier, rival explanation, stopping boundary and successor interface. The counts describe publication architecture, not experimentally verified results or independently certified scientific originality. The Ten Research Directions F111 Nanorobotic Collective Limited Communication Control At The Limit — Investigates safe collective recovery when peer-to-peer messages are delayed, lost or limited. The proposed endpoint is time to independently confirmed safe recovery after communication loss, measured in seconds. Tests compare matched-actuation single-agent control against local coordination; task redundancy is a rival explanation. Failure to regain a known-safe state is a stopping condition. F112 Microrobotic Collective Quantum Sensing Collaboration At The Limit — Proposes cooperative field sensing against independent calibrated reference measurements. Its candidate endpoint is normalized field-estimation error; the atlas also tracks communication load. A fully observed centralized controller is the comparator, and additional agent count may explain apparent improvement. Violation of registered safety invariants rejects the proposed collaborative sensing benefit. F113 Nanorobotic Collective Consensus Failure At The Limit — Examines whether distributed agreement remains justified when hidden partitions or corrupted information change the swarm's evidence. The candidate endpoint is the false-consensus acceptance fraction, with energy per task retained from the atlas. Fixed rules under equal energy challenge the proposal; leaked global tracking is a rival. Confidence maintained during a hidden partition triggers rejection. F114 Microrobotic Collective Dynamic Mission Reconfiguration At The Limit — Studies bounded mission reassignment following changing tasks, link loss or unavailable agents. The proposed witness is independently verified mission-reassignment success fraction, while selective abstention remains an atlas outcome. Matched total actuation controls for redundancy masquerading as adaptation. Failed return to a registered safe state is the hard stop. F115 Nanorobotic Collective Joint Human-Machine Oversight At The Limit — Tests whether collective task completion remains inside explicit human authorization and machine safety constraints. Authority-compliant task success fraction is the proposed endpoint, complemented by atlas task-completion records. A centralized full-state controller is the comparator; larger teams alone may explain any gain. Crossing a safety invariant overrides apparent task efficiency. F116 Microrobotic Collective Misinformation Propagation At The Limit — Addresses the spread of incorrect shared state estimates through a microrobotic collective. Its candidate observable is false-belief propagation rate, accompanied by the atlas consensus-error outcome. Equal-energy fixed behavior challenges the claimed mechanism, while hidden external state tracking may bias comparisons. Persistent confident agreement under concealed network partition is a rejection condition. F117 Nanorobotic Collective Graceful Degradation At The Limit — Evaluates whether a damaged or partially disconnected swarm retains bounded task capability rather than failing abruptly. Completion fraction under preregistered fault severity is the proposed witness; the atlas also records collision rate. Single-agent operation with matched total actuation tests whether redundancy alone explains resilience. Inability to return to a known-safe state stops the trial. F118 Microrobotic Collective Mission Integrity At The Limit — Proposes end-to-end custody and task-state audits for collective sampling missions. abstract: STARLI | F111–F120 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · Collective Microrobotics, Fault Resilience and Trustworthy Autonomy Author: 33 | Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.2 | English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This collection presents ten prospective research-design monographs on distributed micro/nanorobotic collectives. Research Unit I (F111–F115) addresses limited communication, collaborative quantum sensing, consensus breakdown, dynamic task reassignment and joint human-machine authority. Research Unit II (F116–F120) examines misinformation propagation, graceful degradation, custody and mission integrity, cross-platform coordination and trustworthy autonomy. The ten studies propose falsifiable bench-scale experiments; none asserts demonstrated swarm intelligence, clinical efficacy or certified autonomous safety. The ten English working editions comprise 7,770 PDF pages in total: 300 prospective mathematical research plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study sections, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Gate proposes six annotated research dimensions: causal mechanism, measurable witness, blinded falsifier, rival explanation, stopping boundary and successor interface. The counts describe publication architecture, not experimentally verified results or independently certified scientific originality. The Ten Research Directions F111 Nanorobotic Collective Limited Communication Control At The Limit — Investigates safe collective recovery when peer-to-peer messages are delayed, lost or limited. The proposed endpoint is time to independently confirmed safe recovery after communication loss, measured in seconds. Tests compare matched-actuation single-agent control against local coordination; task redundancy is a rival explanation. Failure to regain a known-safe state is a stopping condition. F112 Microrobotic Collective Quantum Sensing Collaboration At The Limit — Proposes cooperative field sensing against independent calibrated reference measurements. Its candidate endpoint is normalized field-estimation error; the atlas also tracks communication load. A fully observed centralized controller is the comparator, and additional agent count may explain apparent improvement. Violation of registered safety invariants rejects the proposed collaborative sensing benefit. F113 Nanorobotic Collective Consensus Failure At The Limit — Examines whether distributed agreement remains justified when hidden partitions or corrupted information change the swarm's evidence. The candidate endpoint is the false-consensus acceptance fraction, with energy per task retained from the atlas. Fixed rules under equal energy challenge the proposal; leaked global tracking is a rival. Confidence maintained during a hidden partition triggers rejection. F114 Microrobotic Collective Dynamic Mission Reconfiguration At The Limit — Studies bounded mission reassignment following changing tasks, link loss or unavailable agents. The proposed witness is independently verified mission-reassignment success fraction, while selective abstention remains an atlas outcome. Matched total actuation controls for redundancy masquerading as adaptation. Failed return to a registered safe state is the hard stop. F115 Nanorobotic Collective Joint Human-Machine Oversight At The Limit — Tests whether collective task completion remains inside explicit human authorization and machine safety constraints. Authority-compliant task success fraction is the proposed endpoint, complemented by atlas task-completion records. A centralized full-state controller is the comparator; larger teams alone may explain any gain. Crossing a safety invariant overrides apparent task efficiency. F116 Microrobotic Collective Misinformation Propagation At The Limit — Addresses the spread of incorrect shared state estimates through a microrobotic collective. Its candidate observable is false-belief propagation rate, accompanied by the atlas consensus-error outcome. Equal-energy fixed behavior challenges the claimed mechanism, while hidden external state tracking may bias comparisons. Persistent confident agreement under concealed network partition is a rejection condition. F117 Nanorobotic Collective Graceful Degradation At The Limit — Evaluates whether a damaged or partially disconnected swarm retains bounded task capability rather than failing abruptly. Completion fraction under preregistered fault severity is the proposed witness; the atlas also records collision rate. Single-agent operation with matched total actuation tests whether redundancy alone explains resilience. Inability to return to a known-safe state stops the trial. F118 Microrobotic Collective Mission Integrity At The Limit — Proposes end-to-end custody and task-state audits for collective sampling missions. The measurable candidate is the valid sample-and-mission custody fraction, with coverage entropy retained from the original atlas. A centralized full-state controller anchors comparison; increased agent number can mimic benefits. Any violation of physical safety invariants invalidates the release claim. F119 Nanorobotic Collective Cross-Platform Collaboration At The Limit — Studies verified recovery and coordination across dissimilar robotic platforms with distinct sensing and control interfaces. Recovery latency in seconds is the proposed measurement and atlas recovery time is preserved. Matched-energy fixed rules are the baseline; external tracking that reveals global state is a rival. Confident consensus during a hidden communication partition is a stop condition. F120 Intelligent Nanorobotic Collective Trustworthy Autonomy At The Limit — Investigates whether autonomous collective decisions remain within defined authority and physical safety envelopes. The candidate witness is unsafe autonomous release fraction, alongside atlas communication load. A matched-actuation single-agent baseline tests purported benefits of collective intelligence versus redundancy. Failure to recover a known-safe state disqualifies the autonomy claim. The publication title follows the corrected source-introduction identity. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries These nonclinical research-design working editions are limited to traceable materials, calibrated sensing, physically bounded actuation, authorized reference systems and laboratory or simulated validation. Proposed endpoints supplement, rather than silently replace, the original atlas outcome fields. No laboratory results are reported. Equal-resource baselines, blinded disturbance tests, preservation of failed runs, raw evidence provenance and mandatory stop rules are required before claims of superiority. The source batch passes scripted PDF-structure checks; derivation-level physics, causal distinctness, individual DOI-to-claim relevance, exhaustive visual review and specialist peer review remain incomplete. Detailed source-to-claim matching and independent bibliography review remain outstanding. title: Prevalence of Medication and Supplement Use Among Pre-Eligibility Milk Bank Donors: An Australian Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study
authors: Claire Newman; Laura D. Klein; Mitch Booth; Luke E. Grzeskowiak; Vanessa Clifford
abstract: BACKGROUND: Potential milk donors should be carefully screened to ensure that donated human milk is safe for vulnerable infant recipients. Some medications and supplements may result in donor deferral or make donation impossible. However, evidence about medication or supplement exposures among those considering donating excess breast milk in Australia remains limited. AIM: To examine medication and supplement use among pre-eligibility donors to an Australian nonprofit milk bank. METHODS: A retrospective cross-sectional study analyzed 1,480 high-level screening questionnaires completed at the Australian Red Cross Lifeblood milk bank between January 2023 and December 2024. All medications and supplements reportedly taken during the 10 weeks preceding the pre-eligibility donor screening interview were extracted, categorized, and summarized descriptively. RESULTS: Screening occurred a median of 9.7 weeks postpartum. Overall, 90% of pre-eligibility donors reported using either medications (75.2%) or supplements (64.1%), with many using both. Analgesics were most common (taken by 61.9%), followed by anticoagulants (22.1%), antibiotics (14.7%), hormonal therapies (11%), and antihypertensives (7%). Overall, 46.5% reported using at least one short-term medication associated with temporary deferral, and 12.4% were taking a long-term medication at screening that could have led to ineligibility. Multivitamins were the most commonly taken supplement (44.5% of all pre-eligibility donors). CONCLUSIONS: Medications were primarily short-term treatments for postpartum care. Supplement use was prevalent, with multiple products taken. Given the limited safety data for many medications and supplements in the context of donor milk, these findings highlight the need for clearer, evidence-based guidance to support safe and inclusive donor eligibility decisions.

title: Emergency response to COVID‐19 epidemic: One Chinese blood centre's experience
authors: Ping Fang Hu; Jianxun Kang; Ying Li; Xiaochun Li; Meng Li; Min Deng; Yuwei Zhao; Hao Tian; Rui Li; Jie Zhang; Yan Xi; Wen Li; Jialiang Gao; Hua Shan; Xuemei Fu
abstract: OBJECTIVE: The COVID-19 epidemic has caused a significant global social and economic impact since December 2019. The objective of this study was to demonstrate the emergency response of a Chinese blood centre on maintaining both the safety and the sufficiency of blood supply during large, emerging, infectious epidemics. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Early on in the outbreak of COVID-19, the Chengdu Blood Center developed strategies and implemented a series of measures, including enhanced recruitment efforts, addition of new donation deferral criteria and notification after donation, optimisation of donor experience, development and implementation of a new coronavirus nucleic acid detection technology platform for blood screening and screening all donations for SARS-CoV-2 RNA to maximumly protect the safety of blood supply during a time of unclear risk. RESULTS: Starting on February 20, the immediate satisfaction rate of blood product orders in Chengdu city's clinical settings reached 100%, and there was no case of blood transfusion infection. CONCLUSION: The recent experience during the outbreak of SARS-CoV-2 reminded us that improvement in the areas of national and international collaborative programmes for dealing with blood availability and safety concerns during early stages of a disaster and regional and national mechanisms for timely communication with the general public on behalf of blood services should help to better prepare us for future disasters.

title: AUTONOMOUS NANOSCALE REPAIR OF QUANTUM DEVICES AT THE LIMIT Defect Localization, Bounded Nanoscale Intervention, and Independent Quantum Requalification STARLI · White Rainbow Civilization · Research Edition v1.0 ABSTRACT This monograph proposes a falsifiable research architecture for autonomous nanoscale repair of quantum devices. Its governing distinction is between an apparently successful local material action and genuine recovery of quantum-device function under independent requalification. The proposed three-part coupling combines defect localization, bounded nanoscale intervention, and an external quantum-function witness. Local deposition, surface conditioning, annealing, re-alignment, etching, module exchange, and other repair candidates are treated as platform-limited hypotheses, not as universally available capabilities. When defects cannot be identified, an actuator lacks permission, or a proposed step risks irreversible damage, abstention and conservative retirement are legitimate endpoints. The research program separates superconducting circuit interfaces, Josephson junction defects, charge-disordered silicon quantum dots, photonic circuits and photon detectors. It requires causal comparisons against expert maintenance, unchanged fresh-device acceptance thresholds, blinded repair trials, delayed reliability testing, operator-independent metrology, vendor-absent reconstruction and explicit material-history documentation. The proposed 'Quantum Nano Repair Passport' binds defect hypotheses, raw observations, material changes, dose budgets, repair authority, negative evidence, quantum outcomes and remaining-life assessment. An apparent recovery in geometry, frequency or readout settings alone is not conflated with reduction of a causal decoherence mechanism. The architecture includes 30 mathematical derivation plates, 82 chapters with five research sections each, 200 open Research Gates, 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos and 233 named mathematical/physics signposts. The equations are heterogeneous diagnostics, approximations and research criteria, not claims of 233 new physical laws. The proposed experiments have not been performed as part of this book and the integrated repair framework is unvalidated; the work is a theory-and-methods research edition rather than a report of peer-reviewed empirical results. Scientific reference anchors with verified DOI identifiers include: 10.1063/1.4934486 (superconducting surface dielectric participation), 10.1038/s41534-021-00491-2 (surface treatments and coherence), 10.1038/s41534-021-00464-5 (Josephson junction laser trimming), 10.1038/s41534-022-00532-4 (junction two-level defects), 10.1038/s41534-024-00827-8 (Si/SiGe interfacial disorder), 10.1140/epjqt/s40507-017-0064-x (laser annealing of selected photon detectors), and 10.59161/JCGM100-2008E (metrological uncertainty). These sources substantiate physical background, not the integrated autonomous repair hypothesis. STRUCTURE 30 mathematical prelude derivations; 82 research chapters; 410 single-section pages; 200 Research Gates; 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos; 233 individual equation signposts; DOI bibliography; scientific limitations and successor research roadmap. PUBLICATION NOTE An independent, speculative research and reproducibility architecture. Readers should not infer certification of laboratory safety, independent verification, or a functioning autonomous repair system. The author's suggested experiments require separate authorization and specialized laboratory oversight.

title: Personalized Acute Upper GI Bleeding Diagnostics for Patients at Highest Risk for Endoscopy: Real-World Experience of a Novel, Binary, Bedside Gastric Blood Detection Device
authors: Hadi Khaled Abou Zeid; Manik Aggarwal; Jad P. AbiMansour; Miranda M. Hamlin; Yara Salameh; Karl Akiki; Andrew C. Storm
abstract: Background: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) is a common medical emergency associated with significant morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Many patients undergo early endoscopy despite the absence of active bleeding. PillSense is a novel Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared ingestible capsule that rapidly detects the presence of blood in the upper GI tract and may optimize triage decisions. Methods: We conducted a retrospective study evaluating the impact of PillSense on the management of suspected UGIB in an academic center. The primary outcome was the association between capsule results and clinical decision-making, including endoscopy deferral, prioritization, outpatient scheduling, and airway protection. Secondary outcomes included transfusion requirements, time-to-endoscopy, endoscopic intervention, and 30-day adverse events. Results: A total of 28 patients (mean age 64.4 ± 17.9 years, 82.7% male) were included. Compared with negative results, positive results were associated with higher transfusion requirements (median 3 (IQR 3–6) vs. 2 (IQR 1–3.25) units; p = 0.041) and shorter time-to-endoscopy (median 0.2 (IQR 0.01–1) vs. 2 (IQR 1–15.5) days; p = 0.017). In high-risk for sedated endoscopy patients, negative results were associated with EGD deferral in 53.8%, with no subsequent adverse events within 30 days. Endoscopic intervention was performed in 62.5% of positive-result patients versus 9.5% of negative-result patients. Conclusions: The PillSense results were associated with differences in triage and management of high-risk patients with suspected UGIB. Its rapid, accurate, and non-invasive results may reduce unnecessary urgent endoscopy procedures, improve resource utilization, and enhance patient safety, particularly in the highest-risk populations.

title: Rare Cause of Recurrent Deep Vein Thrombosis of the Lower Limbs in a Young Adult Woman Aged 21: Intestinal Malrotation a Case Report from Nianankoro Fomba Regional Hospital of Segou (HNF/S), Discovered in 2023
authors: Boua Daoud Camara; Dramane Traoré; Amadou Kone; Kaly Keita; Djibril Sy; Djénébou Traore; Assétou Soukho Kaya; Mamadou Dembele; Hamar Alassane Traoré
abstract: Presenting in adults, intestinal malrotation is difficult to diagnose, as it manifests itself with atypical symptoms such as chronic, vague abdominal pain and weight loss. Radiological correlation is often essential to diagnose these patients. For surgical intervention, a laparoscopic approach is considered best in expert hands. Even if the disease is chronic, great care should be taken when treating intestinal malrotation in adult men. Timely surgery can work wonders and prevent catastrophic complications. Interrupting the 90° intestinal rotation with reintegration and abutments results in a position where the entire small intestine, including the duodenojejunal angle, is located on the right of the spine, while the entire colon is on the left. Vascular complications are dominated by ischemia of the mesenteric artery and occasionally thrombosis of the mesenteric vein. Deep vein thrombosis of the lower limbs secondary to intestinal malrotation is an exceptional occurrence. To our knowledge, we report the only case in the literature. Conclusion: If the diagnosis of intestinal malrotation is made late, surgical intervention may be life threatening; in our patient, surgical abstention was observed.

title: StreamSense: Streaming Social Task Detection with Selective Vision-Language Model Routing
authors: Han Wang; Deyi Ji; Lanyun Zhu; Jiebo Luo; Roy Ka-Wei Lee
abstract: Live streaming platforms require real-time monitoring and reaction to social signals, utilizing partial and asynchronous evidence from video, text, and audio. We propose StreamSense, a streaming detector that couples a lightweight streaming encoder with selective routing to a Vision-Language Model (VLM) expert. StreamSense handles most timestamps with the lightweight streaming encoder, escalates hard/ambiguous cases to the VLM, and defers decisions when context is insufficient. The encoder is trained using (i) a cross-modal contrastive term to align visual/audio cues with textual signals, and (ii) an IoU-weighted loss that down-weights poorly overlapping target segments, mitigating label interference across segment boundaries. We evaluate StreamSense on multiple social streaming detection tasks (e.g., sentiment classification and hate content moderation), and the results show that StreamSense achieves higher accuracy than VLM-only streaming while only occasionally invoking the VLM, thereby reducing average latency and compute. Our results indicate that selective escalation and deferral are effective primitives for understanding streaming social tasks. Code is publicly available on GitHub.

title: TITLE AUTONOMOUS SELF-REPAIRING ROBOTIC SWARMS AT THE LIMIT SUBTITLE Distributed Intelligence, Causal Fault Diagnosis, Reversible Repair, and Independent Requalification AUTHOR Feng Cheng-en (33) x STARLI Research Institute XXVII ENGLISH PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION What would count as genuine repair in a robot swarm? Mission continuation is not enough. A swarm may route around a damaged agent, reduce an unannounced requirement, sacrifice unmeasured capability, or transfer risk to its neighbors while appearing successful. Autonomous Self-Repairing Robotic Swarms at the Limit develops a falsifiable research architecture for distributed fault detection, causal diagnosis, risk isolation, reversible intervention, task redistribution, physical and morphological repair, and independent post-repair requalification. The central claim is deliberately bounded: when fault genealogy, capability envelopes, uncertainty-aware local evidence, reversible action, and independent qualification operate together, local repair should improve functional recovery without increasing latent failure. The monograph contains thirty linked research equations, eighty-two chapters with five substantial research sections each, and two hundred detailed Research Gates. Every gate specifies a question, registered hypothesis, minimum experiment, observables, strong baseline, falsifier, stopping rule, successor evidence package, and DOI anchors. The single-section / single-page architecture makes each research unit independently addressable and suitable for future human and AI reconstruction. The book separates repair from redundancy, rerouting, graceful degradation, replacement, and self-certification. It examines gradual and abrupt faults, common-cause failure, partial observability, calibration drift, network partition, Byzantine behavior, docking and connector fatigue, repair-induced damage, predictive maintenance, residual-life estimation, blind fault injection, withheld missions, human override, cybersecurity, vendor independence, retirement, and cross-generational handoff. Evidence is anchored in modular reconfigurable robotics, swarm fault diagnosis, self-healing collectives, resilient coordination, distributed metrology, and safe swarm design. The equations are transparent design heuristics rather than universal physical laws, and the integrated system remains a research hypothesis. Unknown states must trigger abstention; the repairer cannot be the sole verifier; moving thresholds invalidate success; irreversible harm and failed override are hard stops. This volume is written for robotics researchers, systems engineers, safety and verification specialists, autonomous-systems designers, AI researchers, and future successors who need not merely a vision of self-healing machines, but a testable path for deciding when a swarm has truly restored function - and when it must stop. title: Trajectories of Mental Health Problems in Childhood and Adult Voting Behaviour: Evidence from the 1970s British Cohort Study
authors: Lisa‐Christine Girard; Martin Okolikj
abstract: Abstract The link between childhood mental health difficulties such as conduct problems and adult political abstention has been overlooked despite early mental health difficulties potentially resulting in political self-marginalisation. Using the1970s British Cohort Study, we estimate developmental trajectories of conduct problems (i.e., from 5 to 16 years). Logistic regression, linear probability models, and propensity score matching were then conducted to test the association between trajectory group membership and voter turnout at 30, 42, and 46 years of age. Three distinct trajectories of conduct problems were identified: a normative (n = 11,871; reference group), moderate-chronic (n = 3433), and elevated-chronic (n = 250) group. Results revealed an association between conduct problems and decreased turnout. In particular the elevated-chronic group had a decreased odds of voting of 52.2%, 52.0%, and 45.7%, as compared to the normative group at 30, 42, and 46 years respectively. The moderate-chronic group had a decreased odds of voting of 24.7% as compared to the normative group at age 30 only. Matched results and linear probability models substantiated findings, suggesting (1) the importance of considering childhood factors when examining antecedents of lifelong voting behaviour, and (2) the political self-marginalisation of people with chronic childhood conduct problems more than 3 decades later.

title: Multiangle Roadside Video Driven School Zone Traffic Conflict Recognition Using a PatchTST Informer Model
authors: Nikola Šarić; Bruno Kraljević; Valentin Živković
abstract: School entrances concentrate pedestrian crossings, vehicle turning movements, and temporary stopping within a restricted observation area. Reliable conflict recognition requires complementary camera coverage and timely representation of changing interactions. This paper proposes a trajectory-based framework combining confidence weighted multiview fusion, a patch time series Transformer, and an Informer context encoder. Synchronized roadside observations are projected onto a common ground plane, associated across views, and represented through motion, separation, visibility, and crossing context. A local branch encodes overlapping temporal patches, while a sparse attention branch represents longer interaction histories. A gated classifier combines these representations to provide calibrated event probabilities. The evaluation protocol specifies 12,000 interaction episodes across twelve school settings, including a school disjoint test partition containing 3,000 episodes. At the selected operating point, the test counts comprise 819 true positives, 81 false negatives, 105 false positives, and 1,995 true negatives, corresponding to 88.64% precision, 91.00% recall, and 89.80% F1. Additional diagnostics examine occlusion, patch length, calibration, selective prediction, and processing budgets. The numerical assessment connects recognition performance with observation quality and the operational requirements of the proposed pipeline. The contribution concerns their integration for event-level recognition; the reported classification metrics quantify agreement with the conflict annotation rule. Processing budgets and calibration diagnostics require separate verification before operational deployment. The framework provides a methodological specification for school zone conflict recognition by separating trajectory uncertainty, temporal representation, and alert decisions. Independent field validation is required to assess generalizability and operational performance.

title: Why I do not treat patients for mild disease
authors: Christophe Hézode
abstract: The short-term prognosis of patients with chronic hepatitis C and mild disease is excellent. Monitoring of the progression of fibrosis is easy to perform with non-invasive tests. Current all-oral interferon (IFN)- and ribavirin (RBV)-free regimens offer sustained viral response (SVR) rates of more than 90% as well as 12-weeks of treatment for most patients with mild disease. Several DAA combinations can be selected to optimize efficacy and safety outcomes. A short treatment duration of 8 weeks could be indicated in most patients with mild disease. However, additional data from clinical trials and real-life experience are needed to confirm this option. Moreover, current regimens are not cost-effective for patients with mild disease. In practice, deferral of HCV treatment for a few years and monitoring the progression of fibrosis is a safe option until cheaper, shorter, more effective and more convenient HCV regimens become available.

title: Measuring Lung Cancer Screening Volume and Adherence During the COVID-19 Pandemic
authors: Christine S. Shusted; Hee‐Soon Juon; Brooke M. Ruane; B. Jackson; Charnita M Zeigler-Johnson; Russell K. McIntire; Gregory C. Kane; Nathaniel Rutherford Evans; Julie A. Barta
venue: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
abstract: RATIONALE: Although lung cancer screening (LCS) uptake has increased to 5-16% nationally, screening initiation and adherence rates are threatened by the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. Consistent with guidelines from a CHEST expert panel, our LCS program deferred new and annual low-dose CT (LDCT) screens during the pandemic's spring surge. Upon resuming screening, we pivoted to shared decision-making (SDM) via telemedicine. We characterized how these changes in screening implementation impacted our LCS volume and adherence. METHODS: We measured LCS patient- and LDCT scan-related volumes through our centralized program during pre-COVID (2019), deferral (March 18-May 18, 2020), and follow-up (May 18-November 18, 2020) to measure 3 outcomes: 1). Monthly volume of LDCTs in 2020 compared to 2019, 2). LDCT completion rate for SDM via telemedicine during the follow-up period, and 3). Adherence rates among patients due for LDCT during the deferral period and returned in the subsequent 6 months, compared to adherence among pre-COVID LCS patients. Adherence was defined as a subsequent CT within 11-18 months of a Lung-RADS 1 or 2 result, 4-8 months for Lung-RADS 3, and 2.5-4.5 months for Lung-RADS 4 patients recommended for 3-month follow-up. RESULTS: Monthly scan volume in our LCS program decreased during the COVID-19 first wave but increased following resumption of screening, and by August, the number of LDCTs exceeded 2019 (Figure). The number of patients screened between May-November 2020 and May-November 2019 was comparable (491 and 505 patients, respectively). However, the frequency of patients returning for follow-up was higher in 2020 compared with 2019 (62.1% vs. 46.3%). Following implementation of telemedicine, the screening completion rate decreased during May-November 2020, with 88.6% of patients (435/491) completing SDM but not LDCT, compared with 100% between May-November 2019. During the deferral period March-May 2020, 124 patients were due for a follow-up scan, and 54 (43.5%) received their scan within the study period. In comparison, 60.3% due for follow-up during the same period in 2019 completed their scan. CONCLUSIONS: Maintaining screening adherence has become a focus for many LCS programs. We observed that following the spring surge of the COVID-19 pandemic, the frequency of returning patients was greater than that of new patients initiating screening. Conducting SDM via telemedicine may introduce a barrier to LCS completion. Adherence rates decreased from 2019, with the lowest rates among Lung-RADS 3 patients due for a 6-month follow-up. Additional research should test LCS implementation strategies to improve adherence during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Rubric-Conditioned LLM Grading: Alignment, Uncertainty, and Robustness
authors: Haotian Deng; Chris Farber; Jiyoon Lee; David Tang
abstract: Automated short-answer grading (ASAG) remains a challenging task due to the linguistic variability of student responses and the need for nuanced, rubric-aligned partial credit. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising solution, their reliability as automated judges in rubric-based settings requires rigorous assessment. In this paper, we systematically evaluate the performance of LLM-judges for rubric-based short-answer grading. We investigate three key aspects: the alignment of LLM grading with expert judgment across varying rubric complexities, the trade-off between uncertainty and accuracy facilitated by a consensus-based deferral mechanism, and the model's robustness under random input perturbations and adversarial attacks. Using the SciEntsBank benchmark and Qwen 2.5-72B, we find that alignment is strong for binary tasks but degrades with increased rubric granularity. Our "Trust Curve" analysis demonstrates a clear trade-off where filtering low-confidence predictions improves accuracy on the remaining subset. Additionally, robustness experiments reveal that while the model is resilient to prompt injection, it is sensitive to synonym substitutions. Our work provides critical insights into the capabilities and limitations of rubric-conditioned LLM judges, highlighting the importance of uncertainty estimation and robustness testing for reliable deployment.

title: An Open-Source Two-Stage Computer Vision Pipeline for Fine-Grained Vehicle Classification using Vision Transformers
authors: Gandhimathi Padmanaban; Fred Feng
abstract: Vehicle body type is a significant determinant of cyclist injury severity in overtaking crashes, yet automated tools for classifying vehicles into injury-risk-relevant categories from naturalistic roadway video do not exist in the open literature. Standard object detection benchmarks provide only coarse vehicle labels (car, truck, bus, motorcycle), while existing fine-grained recognition systems are trained on controlled imagery and lack evaluation for deployment robustness across recording sites. This paper presents an open-source two-stage computer vision pipeline combining a pre-trained RT-DETR detector for coarse vehicle localization with a fine-tuned Vision Transformer (ViT-Base/16) for six-category body-type classification: passenger car, SUV, pickup truck, minivan, large van, and commercial truck. A confidence-based abstention mechanism withholds Stage 2 predictions when softmax output falls below 0.60, producing unknown labels rather than silent misclassifications. Evaluated on 3,805 annotated overtaking events from a bicycle-lane corridor in Ann Arbor, Michigan (in-distribution), the pipeline achieved 0.94 accuracy with per-class F1 scores from 0.91 (minivan) to 0.97 (SUV). On an independent out-of-distribution evaluation of 311 events from an open cycling dataset without retraining, accuracy was 0.89. Three of four well-represented categories maintained F1 at or above 0.90 under domain shift. The largest degradation was observed for minivan (F1 = 0.72), driven by abstention rate rising from 2.4% to 25.0% rather than active misclassification, consistent with the mechanism propagating genuine model uncertainty. The full pipeline, including inference scripts, training code, evaluation utilities, and model weights, is released as open-source software to support reproducibility and reuse across roadside video archives and cycling safety research.

title: EyeSeek: a large language model for screening and improving health literacy in primary eye care
authors: Jieru Liu; Juzhao Zhang; Lianqiang Gan; Yi Xu; Tao Yu; Yajun Peng; Lina Lu; Jingkuan Song; Senlin Lin; Haidong Zou
abstract: Resource constraints and low health literacy hinder the effectiveness of primary eye care screening. Here, we developed EyeSeek, a specialized large language model (LLM) to provide residents with personalized screening interpretations and guidance. We introduced a novel abstention-driven iterative learning framework to enhance reliability by detecting uncertainty, alongside a role-playing strategy for tailored communication. Findings demonstrated that our method can abstain and seek external answers when handling queries beyond its knowledge boundary, which reduces hallucination. In expert evaluation, EyeSeek outperformed several LLMs and primary care physicians in multiple dimensions. Readability analysis confirmed that EyeSeek adapted responses to Grade 3 ~ 8 levels, enabling more accessible communication for residents with varying educational backgrounds. Furthermore, we performed a single-center real-world prospective study comparing referral adherence between the EyeSeek-assisted group ( n = 84) and the unassisted group ( n = 86). The EyeSeek-assisted group demonstrated higher referral adherence ( P = 0.037) and improved health literacy compared with the unassisted group, with high user satisfaction. Given its multifaceted performance, EyeSeek holds promise as an adaptable digital solution to support primary eye care in community settings.

title: Machine Learning in Automation
authors: Jürgen Beyerer; Oliver Niggemann
abstract: In the 21st century, we no longer try to turn lead into gold, but data into money. Machine Learning therefore becomes our modern Philosopher's Stone. While the search for the Philosopher's Stone occupied researchers for 2500 years-leading to porcelain and not to gold-we are optimistic to achieve better results in a shorter period of time. Machine Learning has been an established field of research for decades, yielding a large set of tested algorithms and many successful applications. Nevertheless, the application of these algorithms to Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) is a rather new field which still poses several challenges. First of all, CPS require solutions which fulfil nonfunctional requirements such as safety, security, maintainability and real-time capabilities. They also show a complex timing behavior which is often due to complex causalities and due to state-based system behavior. Furthermore, the number of useful data points is rather small compared to other domains, mainly because the observed data is highly redundant and covers only a few typical normal situations and not much more informative marginal situations. Several solutions to these challenges are currently in the focus of research, e. g., the integration of a priori knowledge into Machine Learning algorithms (i. e., Greybox-Approaches), the automatic configuration and choice of suitable algorithms (i. e., AutoML), or the development of specific algorithms. However, questions such as data quality, big data platforms and time synchronization also play an important role. This special issue will highlight some of these research trends. The question of interpretability is in the focus of the first paper, ""Interpretable machine learning with reject option"". The next paper, ""Combining expert knowledge and unsupervised learning techniques for anomaly detection in aircraft flight data"", deals with the integration of a priori knowledge on the learning methods. The papers ""Computation of energy efficient driving speeds in conveyor systems"" and ""Online parameter estimation for cyber-physical production systems"" outline methods to learn models for the purpose of prediction and optimization. Finally, the papers ""Simulation and optimization of industrial production lines"" and ""Assessment of variance & distribution in data for effective use of statistical methods for product quality prediction"" apply learned models to prediction tasks.

title: Accounting and auditing of credit loss estimates: The hard and the soft
authors: Pablo Pérez Rodríguez
venue: Latin American Journal of Central Banking
abstract: A key goal of financial reporting is to address information asymmetries, which are amplified in the case of banks given their credit, maturity and liquidity transformation and complex, judgmental accounting standards dealing with expected credit losses (ECL). The paper explores the role of bank management in estimating and recognizing ECL, and how external auditors challenge the resulting figures. Based on analysis of G-SIB disclosures, it concludes that management and auditors tend to prioritize observable and verifiable, hard information to reduce challenge to their reported estimates and protect against the threat of legal liability. Emphasis on such information facilitates loss deferral, damaging the reliability of banks’ financial reporting, obscuring their safety and soundness picture and jeopardizing financial stability. Based on these conclusions, the paper seeks to open a new path to the research and policy analysis of credit loss recognition, introducing proposals to address the procyclicality of credit loss accounting by tackling inappropriate incentives that decouple risk taking from its translation onto banks’ financial statements.

title: Monitoring the Spectrum of Donor Deferrals in a Hospital Blood Bank: A Tertiary care Hospital Experience
authors: Attika Khalid; Nazia Khalid; Madeeha Rehan
abstract: Introduction: In an ever-rising need of blood and blood products, donor deferrals not only dent the existing donor pool but also reduces the possibility of further donation by the potential blood donor. This study aims to get an insight into the frequency and causes of deferrals in the region. Methods: This retrospective study was conducted in the blood bank of Fauji Foundation Hospital, Rawalpindi. All the potential donors were evaluated on the basis of clinical history, physical examination and Blood count estimation. Blood was collected from the donors that are deemed fit by above criteria and was screened for Malaria, hepatitis B, C, HIV and syphilis. Results: Out of the total 4225 potential donors 26 (0.61%) were females, 1988 (47%) were in the age range 15-30 years. Of the total potential donors 9.7% donors (410) were deferred. Amongst the deferred, 64% were deferred pre-donation during initial history taking and examination. Amongst the pre-donation deferrals the most common cause was anemia (52.4%) followed by leukocytosis (19.7%) and thrombocytopenia (4.8%) respectively. Post donation deferrals included those patients who showed seropositivity to either hepatitis B, C, HIV, malaria or syphilis. It comprised of 34% of the total deferrals. Hepatitis B was the most common cause of post donation deferral comprising about 49.6% followed by hepatitis C (46%). Only 05 HIV positive cases reported. Conclusion: The analysis of rate and causes of donor deferral may help not only in preventing the donor loss but also in initiating the recruitment efforts and establishing general awareness campaign regarding safety and benefits of donation process at a mass level to help mobilizing voluntary donors from both genders.
