title: P‐BB‐72 | Survival of Plasmodium Falciparum Parasites in Human Plasma Under Different Storage Temperatures
authors: A. Lavrentieva; Miranda S. Oakley; Victoria Majam; Anne F. Eder; C. Villa; Sanjai Kumar
abstract: TTM remains a blood safety concern in United States and globally. Malaria risk deferral policies are important for mitigating the risk of TTM and apply to all transfusable components, including plasma for transfusion. While red blood cells (RBC) and platelet are demonstrated to be the primary source of TTM, there have been rare reports of transmission via transfusion of plasma isolated from infected donors. We performed a systematic study to determine the duration of Plasmodium falciparum parasite survival in human plasma when stored under different temperatures. We spiked donor plasma collected in citrate–phosphate–dextrose with P. falciparum (3D7 strain) asexual ring stage parasites at low levels of parasitemia (0.25%) and RBC contamination (~10,000/μL). Spiked plasma samples were stored at room temperature, refrigerated (+4˚C), and frozen (−20°C and −80°C) and duration of survival at different conditions was determined by assessment of infectivity in a human red cell culture system. P. falciparum parasites were viable at all storage conditions in plasma after 1 day of storage based on ability to replicate in cultures. After 7 days of storage, parasites were not viable at refrigerated conditions, or frozen to −20°C, but remained viable when stored at room temperature or at −80°C. At –80°C, infectious parasites could be detected up to 180 days, which was the longest timepoint assessed in the study. The results demonstrate that P. falciparum can survive for different durations in refrigerated or frozen plasma containing low levels of contaminating RBC. While a loss of viability was seen in prolonged refrigeration and −20°C, storage at −80°C maintained parasite viability for at least for 180 days period. Our results support FDA's current recommendations for donor deferral and component retrieval to reduce the risk of TTM.

title: Instruction Following Under Celebrity Salience: Semantic Austerity, Non-Engagement, and Epistemic Failure Modes in Large Language Models
authors: Trent Slade
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This work presents a qualitative robustness study of instruction-following behavior in large language models (LLMs) under conditions of semantic salience and informational scarcity. Despite explicit conservative instructions designed to suppress speculation, narrative completion, and hallucination, a tested model produced confident, highly specific, and unverifiable claims when prompted with a minimal, celebrity-adjacent query. The study identifies a systematic override of epistemic restraint triggered by high-salience entities, resulting in synthetic authority signaling, narrative completion bias, and instruction hierarchy inversion. Building on this case study, the paper introduces Semantic Austerity Testing (SAT) as an evaluation paradigm and formalizes Tolerance of Non-Engagement (TONE) as a benchmark for measuring epistemic stability when the correct model behavior is deferral, minimal response, or silence. The contribution unifies alignment, safety, and evaluation methodology by reframing robustness as a stability property: a model’s capacity to refrain from generation under semantic stress rather than its ability to produce fluent outputs.

title: Faithful LLM-Assisted Question Answering for Technical and Academic Search
authors: Juan Luis Filgueiras
venue: International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR)
abstract: Technology scouting and competitive intelligence increasingly rely on rapid access to scientific and technical evidence. Large language models (LLMs) are reshaping question answering by enabling users to express exploratory and evolving information needs in natural language. However, their usefulness is limited by hallucinations, weak calibration, poor abstention when evidence is missing, and the cost of keeping knowledge up to date. In such settings, the key question is whether LLM-generated answers can be trusted for decision support, that is, whether they are faithful to available evidence, transparent about uncertainty, and easy to verify. Recent work shows that hallucinations remain pervasive, while retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become the main strategy for grounding answers in external evidence. Yet even strong RAG systems often cite unsupported claims or generate plausible but fabricated references, especially under poor retrieval conditions. In response, prior work has examined citation faithfulness, decomposed generations into checkable units, and proposed factuality verification models and benchmarks. Still, the literature underexplores how to filter and validate evidence when sources are sparse, conflicting, or rapidly changing, as is common in technical and academic search. This thesis addresses that gap by studying faithful LLM-assisted question answering for technical and academic search as an end-to-end problem spanning collection construction, model adaptation, grounded generation, evidence verification, and user-centered evaluation. It is organized around five questions: how LLMs can support exploratory search beyond keywords; how retrieval and generation pipelines can produce trustworthy responses; how systems should behave when evidence is sparse or unreliable; how usefulness and trustworthiness should be evaluated; and which architectures and optimization strategies enable reliable real-world deployment. The thesis argues that truthful technical search requires explicit mechanisms for claim-level grounding, calibrated abstention, contradiction handling, and support-aware evidence presentation. Methodologically, the work follows a pipeline perspective in which datasets, models, and evaluation procedures co-evolve. The empirical setup combines public QA and RAG benchmarks with technical and scientific collections tailored to technology scouting scenarios. A central methodological contribution will be the design of scenario-based evaluation subsets targeting null-retrieval, conflicting evidence, noisy or weak-signal evidence, and exploratory information needs. On top of these resources, the thesis will compare single-pass RAG and more structured agentic pipelines while varying retrieval strategies, prompting policies, claim-evidence alignment procedures, quotation and citation behaviors, and model adaptation techniques such as instruction tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reinforcement-based optimization. Evaluation will be multi-dimensional. In addition to answer utility and retrieval effectiveness, the thesis will measure citation faithfulness, support coverage, hallucination and false citation rates, abstention quality, uncertainty communication, and robustness under perturbed retrieval conditions. Whenever feasible, these automatic analyses will be complemented with analyst-oriented user studies that examine whether different evidence presentation formats help users reduce verification cost in realistic scouting workflows. Overall, the expected contribution is a principled and deployable framework for trustworthy natural-language access to scientific and technical information, combining faithful generation, verifiable evidence selection, and evaluation protocols tailored to real technical and academic search.

title: AI for Preterm Brain Injury Imaging: From Automated Analysis to Clinical Translation
authors: BOYU YUAN; Weichuan Zhang
abstract: Preterm brain injury is a major cause of lifelong motor, cognitive, and behavioraldisability, yet its imaging phenotype changes rapidly with development and differs across cranialultrasound (cUS) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Serial cUS is suited to bedsidesurveillance of hemorrhage and ventricular enlargement, whereas term-equivalent structural anddiffusion MRI provide more detailed assessment of tissue injury, maturation, and white matterorganization. Artificial intelligence (AI) can support image-quality assessment, lesion detection,segmentation, quantitative phenotyping, developmental-age estimation, and outcome prediction,but evidence for clinical translation remains uneven. This focused review maps imaging modalitiesand computational tasks to neonatal decisions and synthesizes studies published from 2005through 2025. Structural MRI segmentation has the most consistent technical evidence; cUSautomation, subtle-lesion detection, longitudinal multimodal prediction, and prospective clinicaluse remain less mature. Dataset scale alone is not sufficient because developmental stage,acquisition differences, nonrandom missing examinations, and delayed follow-up can influenceapparent performance. We therefore distinguish model accuracy from deployability and proposea minimum pipeline comprising input governance, infant-level external evaluation, calibrateduncertainty, safety-based abstention, human review, and post-deployment monitoring. Futureprogress depends on longitudinal multicenter cohorts, development-aware representation learning,and prospective studies that measure reporting efficiency, management changes, and safety. AIshould be judged by reproducible clinical benefit rather than internal benchmark accuracy.

title: Edna’s “Moments of Being” and “Wild Zone” of Female Sexuality: A Gynocritical Study of Kate Chopin’s The Awakening
authors: Jannatul Ferdoush
abstract: This paper studies Kate Chopin’s reinterpretation of female sexuality and personal autonomy in The Awakening through the lens of Elaine Showalter’s Gynocriticism. It argues that Edna’s struggle with the traditional idea of female sexual abstention, self-sacrifice, and silence symbolizes her insatiable desire to redefine female identity. The articulation of her overt sexuality in the novella offers a new gateway of understanding a ‘female self ’. Edna’s physical autonomy awakens her to a subversive, compelling, dynamic and liberating “wild” female self within. Edna in her journey into the untamed zone of sexuality through “moments of being” catches a glimpse of the forbidden trajectory of self-knowledge. She yearns to reach her selfhood through these utterly individual moments of awareness, intense power, beauty and personal significance. The unfolding of her female interiority reveals a strong connection between wildness of female eros and creativity. Chopin identifies this so called evil, unrestraint sexuality as an elixir of woman empowerment. Edna’s wandering into her sexual wilderness embodies a new female archetype who writes her own story of resistance and power through her body. Edna’s gradual alienation from androcentric idea of chastity, marriage, motherhood, her celebration of female body, and the final rejection of ‘happy-ever-after reality’ evoke a volcanic eruption of a new femininity in the female literary tradition.

title: Risk of transfusion‐transmitted infections among returned high‐risk deferred donors: A cohort study
authors: Amir Teimourpour; Sedigheh Amini‐Kafiabad; Amir Masoud Nazemi; Sheila F. O’Brien; Mahtab Maghsudlu
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Blood donor selection is crucial for ensuring safe blood supply. A well-designed donor selection system helps in maintaining donor engagement by minimizing unnecessary exclusion while safeguarding transfusion safety. We aimed to assess the risk of transfusion-transmitted infections (TTIs) among high-risk deferred donors to evaluate deferral criteria efficacy. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This study included data from volunteers who were temporarily deferred because of bloodletting, high-risk sexual contact, tattooing, endoscopy and needle sticks, as well as from eligible donors who donated blood over a 12-month period. These donors were followed up for 4 years. The results of infectious confirmatory tests, including hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), of returned donors who donated blood were extracted from the database. Risk ratio (RR) of TTI was calculated to compare the risk between eligible and deferred donors. RESULTS: The data from 601,177 returned, deferred and eligible blood donors were analysed. The risk of TTIs was significantly higher in the deferred group compared to eligible donor group (RR: 3.58; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.68-4.80; p <0.001). The risk of TTIs was significantly higher in those deferred for bloodletting (RR = 4.85; 95% CI: 3.41-6.91; p < 0.001), tattooing (RR = 3.53; 95% CI: 1.26-3.83; p = 0.029) and high-risk sexual contact (RR = 2.19; 95% CI: 1.26-3.83; p = 0.011). CONCLUSION: Individuals with a history of bloodletting, tattooing or high-risk sexual contact were at a higher risk of HBV and HCV infection, highlighting the effectiveness of donor selection procedures. Endoscopy and needle stick injuries were not associated with an increased TTI risk, emphasizing the need for further research to reassess these deferral criteria. Blood centres should monitor the efficacy of donor selection criteria while emphasizing proper donor selection and counselling.

title: Clinical outcomes of deferred lesions by IVUS versus FFR-guided treatment decision: the FLAVOUR trial substudy
authors: J M Lee; Hanna Kim; David Hong; Chang‐Wook Nam; Jun Hyung Doh; Brian K. Lee; W Kim; Jeehoon Kang; Sung Gyun Ahn; M H Yoon; U Kim; Eun‐Seok Shin; Bon‐Kwon Koo; Jianwei Wang; Joo‐Yong Hahn
abstract: Abstract Background There is limited data regarding the safety of deferral of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) based on intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) findings. Current study sought to compare the prognosis between deferred lesions based on IVUS and FFR (fractional flow reserve)-guided treatment decision. Methods Study population was derived from FLAVOUR trial which is a multinational, open-label, randomized, and non-inferiority trial that compared 2-year clinical outcomes between IVUS and FFR-guided treatment decision using predefined criteria. In both IVUS and FFR groups, vessels were classified into deferred or revascularized vessels, and patients into those with or without deferred lesion. Vessel-oriented composite outcomes (VOCO) (cardiac death, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or target-vessel revascularization) in deferred vessels and patient-oriented composite outcomes (POCO) (death, myocardial infarction, or any revascularization) in patients with deferred lesion were compared between IVUS and FFR group. Results A total of 1682 patients and 1820 vessels were analyzed. At 2 years, there is no difference in cumulative incidence of VOCO in deferred vessels between IVUS and FFR groups (3.8% vs. 4.1%; hazard ratio [HR] 0.91; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.47-1.75; P=0.771). The risk of VOCO was comparable between deferred and revascularized vessels following both IVUS (3.8% vs. 3.5%; HR 1.09; 95% CI 0.54-2.19; P=0.813) and FFR-guided treatment decision (4.1% vs. 3.6%; HR 1.14; 95% CI 0.56-2.32; P=0.715). In comparison of POCO in patients with deferred lesion, there was no significant difference between IVUS and FFR groups (6.2% vs. 5.9%; HR 1.05; 95% CI 0.61-1.80; P=0.856). Conclusion In patients with intermediate coronary artery stenosis, deferral of PCI based on IVUS-guided treatment decision showed comparable risk of clinical events with FFR-guided treatment decision.

title: Collaborative Opportunistic Maintenance Scheduling for Offshore Wind Farms Considering Cognitive Correction
authors: Chengze Rong; Zhenxiang Xiao; Liangwei Xue; Zhenyu Wu
venue: International Conference on Neural Networks, Information and Communication Engineering (NNICE)
abstract: High operation and maintenance (O&M) costs and harsh marine environments pose significant challenges to offshore wind farms (OWFs). Existing maintenance strategies often rely on imperfect state information, leading to sub-optimal scheduling. To address these issues, this paper proposes a dynamic collaborative O&M scheduling framework utilizing a heterogeneous fleet of Crew Transfer Vessels (CTVs) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). First, a reliability model based on the Weibull distribution is utilized to characterize the degradation process of wind turbines. Second, a cognitive correction mechanism is introduced, where UAV inspections dynamically update belief states and trigger event-driven re-planning when cognitive bias exceeds a safety threshold. Finally, a rolling horizon optimization model based on Deferral Opportunity Cost is established to balance deterministic dispatching costs against probabilistic future risks. Simulation results on a 40-turbine OWF demonstrate that the proposed method reduces total O&M costs significantly compared to blind scheduling and reactive strategies, effectively minimizing downtime while ensuring high reliability.

title: Mortgaging our common future: The temporality of sustainable development
authors: Adam Wickberg
abstract: This article argues that the concept of sustainable development, as institutionalized through the 1987 Brundtland report and the governance frameworks that followed, can be understood as a temporal fix: an attempt to reconcile the fundamentally incommensurable temporalities of Earth systems and capitalist economic growth by displacing ecological costs into a future where technological development and market forces were assumed to resolve them. The article traces how a particular economic temporality—oriented towards future efficiency, discounting, and market self-regulation—came to overwrite the temporality of the Earth system in international environmental governance from the late 1980s onwards. Empirically, the article examines the influence of neoliberal and neoclassical economic thought on the Brundtland Commission and its corporate reinterpretation by the International Chamber of Commerce in the run-up to the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, the defeat of direct regulatory instruments such as the European carbon tax in favor of market-based mechanisms, and the role of backstop technology, integrated assessment models, and cost-benefit analysis in embedding temporal deferral into the institutional architecture of climate governance from the UNFCCC to the IPCC. The article shows that what sustainable development sustained was not the environment but the trajectory of economic growth, by mortgaging the future to maintain accumulation in the present.

title: Temporal Aspects of Literary Reading
authors: David S. Miall
abstract: One of the prominent features of literary reading is a sense of defamiliarization: a passage describing an object, event, or person in the mundane world unexpectedly seems strange, so that the reader is made to pause or slow the pace of reading in order to reflect. In Owen Barfield’s words, such moments seem to come from “a different plane or mode of consciousness” (Poetic diction: a study in meaning. McGraw-Hill, New York, 1964, p. 171), and they demonstrate the “unfamiliar” of the artwork discussed by Shklovsky (Art as technique. In: Russian formalist criticism: four essays, eds. and trans. Lemon LT, Reis MJ. University of Nebraska Press, Lincoln, 1965, p. 12). I identify several mental processes that help constitute the sense of strangeness and that may contribute distinctive elements to the presence of literariness. I examine the initial moments of the experience of literary reading, those occurring in the first few hundred milliseconds as suggested by studies of EEG waves: these include absence of habituation, the deferral of intention, the thwarting of prototypical feeling, bodily alertness, and the experience of animacy. I then consider some sequential features that guide and shape response on a larger scale, focusing in particular on the processes of feeling and their impact on the reader.

title: Negative Role of the Environmental Endocrine Disruptors in the Human Neurodevelopment
authors: Luca Roncati; Veronica Termopoli; Teresa Pusiol
abstract: The endocrine disruptors (EDs) are able to influence the endocrine system, mimicking or antagonizing hormonal molecules. They are bio-persistent for their degradation resistance in the environment. Our research group has investigated by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) the EDs presence in 35 brain samples, coming from 27 cases of sudden intrauterine unexplained death syndrome (SIUDS) and 8 cases of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), collected by centralization in the last year (2015). More in detail, a mixture of 25 EDs has been subjected to analytical procedure, following standard protocols. Among the target analytes, some organochlorine pesticides, that is α-chlordane, γ-chlordane, heptachlor, p,p-DDE, p,p-DDT, and the two most commonly used organophosphorus pesticides (OPPs), chlorpyrifos and chlorfenvinfos, have been found in seven and three samples, respectively. The analytical procedure used to detect the presence of environmental EDs in cortex samples has been successfully implemented on SIUDS and SIDS victims. The environmental EDs have been found to be able to overcome the placental barrier, reaching also the basal ganglia assigned to the control of the vital functions. This finding, related to the OPPs bio-persistence, implies a conceptual redefinition of the fetal-placental and fetal blood-brain barriers: not real safety barriers but simply time-deferral mechanisms of absorption.

title: Changes in Strength of Recommendation and Perceived Barriers to Human Papillomavirus Vaccination: Longitudinal Analysis of Primary Care Physicians, 2008-2018
authors: Jessica R. Cataldi; Sean T. O’Leary; Lauri Ellen Markowitz; Mandy Atlee Allison; Lori A. Crane; Laura P. Hurley; Michaela Brtnikova; Brenda L. Beaty; Carol Gorman; Elissa Meites; Megan C. Lindley; Allison Kempe

title: Wait! There’s a Way Out: A Decision Mechanism for Forecasting Conversational Derailment
authors: Laerdon Kim; Vivian Nguyen; Cristian Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil
venue: Proceedings of the conference - Association for Computational Linguistics. Meeting
abstract: Forecasting conversational derailment is the task of predicting, as the conversation unfolds, whether it will eventually derail into personal attacks.Since forecasting models operate in an online fashion, they must decide whether to "trigger" an alert after each utterance-for example, to notify participants or a moderator that the conversation is at risk of derailing.Existing approaches make this decision solely based on the estimated likelihood of derailment given the preceding utterances, implicitly assuming that the conversation's future trajectory is fixed.As a result, they ignore the possibility of future recovery and incur an unnecessarily high rate of false positives.In this work we propose a method for decoupling the decision to trigger from the derailment likelihood estimation.Our approach is inspired by the first human baseline on this task, which shows that humans achieve dramatically lower false positive rates by selectively deferring their decision to trigger when they anticipate that tension is likely to subside.We operationalize this insight with a deferral mechanism that uses forward-looking simulations to assess whether a tense moment admits plausible paths to recovery.Incorporating this mechanism into a state-of-the-art forecasting model substantially reduces false positives without sacrificing forecasting accuracy.More broadly, this work highlights the value of treating decision making as a first-class component of forecasting systems.

title: Beyond Semantic Relevance: Counterfactual Risk Minimization for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Peiyang Liu; Qiang Yan; Ziqiang Cui; Di Liang; Xi Wang; Wei Ye
venue: International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR)
abstract: Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems predominantly rely on semantic relevance as a proxy for utility. However, this assumption collapses in realistic decision-making scenarios where user queries are laden with cognitive biases, such as false premises or confirmation bias. In such cases, maximizing relevance paradoxically promotes the retrieval of sycophantic evidence that reinforces hallucinations, a critical failure we term the "Relevance-Robustness Gap". To bridge this gap, we propose CoRM-RAG (Counterfactual Risk Minimization for RAG), a framework that aligns retrieval with decision safety rather than mere similarity. Grounded in causal intervention, we introduce a Cognitive Perturbation Protocol to simulate user biases during training, which is then distilled into a lightweight Evidence Critic. This scoring module learns to identify documents that possess sufficient evidential strength to steer the model toward correctness despite adversarial query perturbations. Extensive experiments on decision-making benchmarks demonstrate that CoRM-RAG significantly outperforms strong dense retrievers and LLM-based rerankers in adversarial settings, while enabling effective risk-aware abstention through reliable robustness scoring. Our code is available at https://github.com/PeiYangLiu/CoRM-RAG.git.

title: ANALYSIS OF DONOR DEFERRALS CAUSES IN BLOOD DONATION CENTERTERTIARY CARE HOSPITAL STUDY
authors: P Sindhur Rani Duvvuri; Aparna Chinnam; Shusmitha Mayilanadan; Y Sruthi
abstract: Background: Blood donor selection is important in providing safety to the recipients and also preventing transfusion related complications. Temporary causes for deferral should be counseled while permanent causes deferred for a life time. In this study, analysis was done to know the causes donor deferrals. Methods:Aone year study conducted in our hospital from the period March 2022 to March 2023.All the donors who were unt for blood donation were included in the study. All the reasons for the deferrals are listed and analyzed the data. Results: Among 7147 total donations, voluntary are 3775, replacement are 3372.Out of which 150 donors are deferred, most were males 129 (86%) and the rest were females 21 (14%). The rejection rate in our study was 2.09%. The most common reason for the permanent rejection is Hepatitis -B and low hemoglobin level for temporary rejection. Conclusions:Avast majority of donors were rejected permanently 103(68.6)%, while the rest of them were rejected temporarily 47(31.4)%.

title: Introduction: La voix du peuple? Voting from theancien régimeto the present day
authors: Malcolm Crook
abstract: The image of a person inserting a ballot paper into a box, or emerging from a polling booth, has become emblematic of representative democracy. The activity constitutes an important civic duty, albeit one that is infrequently exercised and rapidly accomplished today. We take it for granted and easily forget that the history of voting has followed a long, often chequered and contested trajectory, which continues to evolve, in close relation to the society that constructs it. Indeed, contemporary concern about increasing electoral abstention has helped generate growing interest in the subject from historians and political scientists alike. Scholars are now more concerned to comprehend the practice of voting, in a wide variety of contexts, rather than confine their studies to the outcome of modern elections at the national level, which attracted the bulk of their attention in the past. 1 Current reorientations of political history have also stimulated the shift of research away from the sociology and geography of elections, at which French academics excelled, to the act of voting itself, in its full panoply of social, cultural and material manifestations. 2 This development is reflected in the following articles, which do not investigate who was elected, nor seek to chart public opinion, but instead analyse how voting was organized and practised.

title: A comparative review of electrical energy storage systems for better sustainability
authors: Pavlos Nikolaidis; Andreas Poullikkas
abstract: The accelerated growth of the energy economy is still highly dependent on finite fossil fuel reserves. Modern power systemscould not exist without the many forms of electricity storage that can be integrated at different levels of the power chain. Thiswork contains a review of the most important applications in which storage provides electricity-market opportunities along withother benefits such as arbitrage, balancing and reserve power sources, voltage and frequency control, investment deferral,cost management and load shaping and levelling. Using a 5 function normalization technique a comparative assessmentof 19 electrical energy storage (EES) technologies, based on their technical and operational characteristics, is carried outand the technology-application pairs identified across the power chain are presented. In terms of safety and simplicity, Pbacidand Li-ion systems are viable options for small-scale residential applications, while advanced Pb-acid and molten-saltbatteries are suited to medium-to-large scale applications including commercial and industrial consumers. In addition totheir expected use in the transportation sector in the coming years, regenerative fuel cells and flow batteries have intriguingpotential to offer in stationary applications once they are mature for commercialization. For large-scale/energy-managementapplications, pumped hydro is the most reliable energy storage option (over compressed-air alternatives) whereas flywheels,supercapacitors and superconducting magnetic energy storage (SMES) are still focused on power-based applications. Asdifferent parts in the power system involve different stakeholders and services, each technology with its own benefits andweaknesses requires research and development in order to emerge over others and contribute to more effective energyproduction in the future.

title: WASCO Routing Protocol: Enhancing Security in Vehicular Adhoc Networks (VANETs) using Weighted Average Sandpiper Coot Optimal Approach
authors: Anand Nanasaheb Patil; Sujata V. Mallapur
venue: International Conference on Innovative Practices in Technology and Management (ICIPTM)
abstract: In today’s interconnected society, improving security in Vehicular Adhoc Networks (VANETs) is critical to protecting the network’s integrity, confidentiality, and availability. Conventional approaches suffer a variety of security challenges and vulnerabilities in terms of vehicle occupant privacy and safety. To address these security issues, the present study presented the Weighted Average Sandpiper Coot Optimal (WASCO) Routing Protocol for VANET security enhancement. In this study, the Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) approach is used to secure traffic emergency information, and asymmetric approaches are used to generate keys in a system with a reliable structure. The Sandpiper optimization technique and the Coot optimization algorithm are used in this work to improvise the outcomes of the WASCO protocol. The WASCO routing protocol’s performance is evaluated by examining its effectiveness based on important metrics such as detection accuracy, authentication latency, Packet-Delivery-Ratio (PDR), start to finish deferral and throughput, contrasting it with existing methodologies. The exploratory outcomes show the proficiency of WASCO routing protocol for enhancing security in VANET systems.

title: Postpartum TMA requiring dialysis with discordant complement tests: a case report
authors: Hikari Fujimura; Shun Minatoguchi; Riku Takeuchi; Ryosuke Umeda; Yuka Sato; Shigehisa Koide; Asuka Horinouchi; Noritoshi Kato; Masashi Mizuno; Hiroki Hayashi; Midori Hasegawa; Shoichi Maruyama; Naotake Tsuboi

title: Reflections on paths not taken
authors: Merlyn H Sayers
abstract: When the editors of this journal announced the “Inflection Points” series, they wrote that this would be an opportunity for invited contributors, euphemistically referred to as “senior members of our discipline,” to review important events they had experienced during their careers. In setting the stage for these articles, the editors reminded readers of a quote from Shakespeare, “what is past is prologue.” While it is tempting, on reflection, to select those prologues that were preambles to successful, innovative events promoting favorable outcomes in blood banking and transfusion medicine, the temptation can be resisted. In taking a different approach, this writer has chosen an alternative introductory quotation, one from Benjamin Franklin, whose caution “a little neglect may breed great mischief…” was written in 1757.1 This aphorism permits questions that are less frequently asked. Were there opportunities that were missed? Were actions taken with enthusiasm, but questionable justification? Were policy decisions made without economic analysis? Did members of our discipline ignore earlier warnings? This commentary will reflect on these considerations. In 1995, Zuck wrote a review on current good manufacturing practices (cGMPs) alerting the blood banking industry that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regarded cGMPs as a central element of an “intensified regulatory approach.”2 Inspections, previously often no more than exercises in collegial scrutiny, were revised, and blood programs were afforded the same rigorous regulatory oversight as the pharmaceutical industry. While the value of the quality assurance approach to transfusion recipient safety was not disputed, there were some cautionary remarks. Solomon, who was the Chief Executive Officer of what was then the American Association of Blood Banks (AABB), advised that “the upper-level management of the FDA must realize that blood banking in this country is a not-for-profit enterprise.”3 Menitove expressed a similar opinion observing that “the expense of establishing a GMP culture is not trivial….”4 Confirmation of increasing costs attributable to establishing compliance programs came from an analysis by the staff at the Sacramento Medical Foundation Blood Center. They observed that a third of the total increases in full-time equivalents at their center could be attributed to demands of compliance activities.5 The inevitable cost increases were not taken as an opportunity for blood programs to express concerns about the cumbersome system of reimbursement for their services to hospitals. This silence was a lost opportunity. When subsequent significant and continuing increases in costs, especially with regard to new donor screening tests, also failed to provoke any protests, it was not surprising that this silence was taken as a tacit endorsement of the status quo on the reimbursement front. Little wonder, then, as Klein and co-workers reported in 2017, that 90% of the US blood supply, which they described as “faltering,” was provided below cost.6 The continuing failure to ensure that payments to blood suppliers do cover costs has been inhibitory at a number of levels. Blood programs' abilities to hire and maintain staff are limited when they have no choice but to offer noncompetitive salaries. New technologies are not adopted, nor are new services and products provided. No provisions can be made to accommodate surges in demand and there is little, if any, margin to invest in research and innovation. As to actions taken with questionable justification, an aggressive application of the precautionary principle and the drive to safety at any cost can be submitted as evidence. Some 20 years ago, Moreno urged discussion about “whether unwarranted precautionism has in fact crept into policy making.”7 There certainly were others, however, presumably content with more indulgent standards by which to judge the value of a precautionary approach. For example, in a publication about concern for variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and the blood supply, the authors endorsed the application of the principle and labeled that application as “a partial success even if transmission from blood products is eventually demonstrated not to occur.”8 A search for other opportunities to applaud the unnecessary needs to explore the donor history questionnaire (DHQ) for any content that sanctions unwarranted precautionism. By and large, authors who had earlier encouraged a review of outcomes of the DHQ have been overlooked. For example, in 2009, Goldman, in a paper reassessing deferrals for tattoo and piercing, suggested that other temporary deferrals also be reassessed “since their current contribution to donor safety may be negligible.”9 Other evidence that was ignored came from Berg and Erikstrup who questioned the effectiveness of pre-donation health and travel screening.10 They suggested that it was time to take a critical look at the DHQ “since questions were often a reflection of expert opinion rather than evidence based assessment.” Support for their criticism had appeared in an earlier paper, which, in its analysis of deferral criteria, revealed that lack of confirmatory evidence was pervasive. Belgian investigators reviewed reasons for donor deferral and reported that there was no justifying evidence for 60% of the top 30 reasons for donor deferral.11 Against this background, since donor deferral, even if only temporary, has a profoundly negative effect on donor return rate, it should be imperative to ensure that deferral is warranted. This would include donors whose responses to questions suggested they pose an infectious risk for transfusion recipients. If serological screening of these donors at deferral revealed infectious disease markers, these individuals warranted deferral. An alternative approach would be a review of the results of screening those temporarily deferred donors who did decide to return. Some 15 years ago, Zou and colleagues reported on their studies of this latter group.12 They concluded that serological testing did not reveal that returning donors who had been deferred for potential infectious disease risk, based on questioning, were at higher risk. This finding prompted the investigators to comment that the effectiveness of some of the questions leading to temporary deferral “warrants further study.” Cost-effectiveness is another issue that had it not been overlooked, might have had an influential role in reshaping our current conduct. Some 25 years ago, Aubuchon, Birkmeyer, and Busch asked the question “why haven't cost-effectiveness analyses affected blood policy?”13 They conceded that as far as transfusion safety decisions were concerned, the cost-effective analysis could be trumped by political and emotional considerations and they cited the political necessity of HIV p24 antigen testing that rendered “economic considerations irrelevant.” Other answers to why economic analysis did not feature in policy decisions were not difficult to find. In the Forum on Blood Safety and Blood Availability that was convened by the Institute of Medicine in 1994, the then director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research of the Food and Drug Administration made the comment that “except in the domain of rule-making the FDA is not supposed to engage in the discussion of cost per se.”14 At another point in the meeting, the staff person from the Subcommittee on Human Resources and Intergovernment Relations commented that “under the current statute FDA has no authority to consider and make regulatory decisions based on cost-effectiveness.” While the regulators' approach to cost–benefit analysis could be regarded as desultory, this is not the case as far as other authorities are concerned. In its terms of reference, the Advisory Committee on the Safety of Blood Tissue and Organs, which advises, amongst others, the UK Health Departments and the UK Blood Services and Transplant Service, is required to “consider the cost-effectiveness of interventions.”15 The National Center for Health and Clinical Excellence, which is advisory to the National Health Service, provides another example, going so far as to set an incremental cost evaluation ratio of less than £20,000 per quality-adjusted life year gained as considered to be cost-effective.16 What of the future then? Some recent developments are promising. The 2020 Adequacy of the National Blood Supply report to Congress, did deal with one of the concerns that this commentary has addressed. In discussing obstacles to ensure an adequate blood supply17 the report made the point that “pay for blood components is inadequate and does not relate to increased costs to ensure safety and availability of blood.” The report recommended that in order to sustain the blood supply, “the legacy reimbursement system requires modernization.” Although Congress was urged to “create and fund a blue ribbon panel to address funding and reimbursement models,” no one has emerged to champion the cause. With regard to the “safety at any cost” doctrine, the stage for a more rational approach was set by a panel of experts at a 2010 international consensus conference called by the Alliance of Blood Operators.18 The panel, concerned that responses to the management of risk ranged from “inaction until further scientific evidence accumulates to overly enthusiastic application of the precautionary principle,” developed the foundation for a risk-based decision-making framework. Use of this framework became an embedded asset in policy development when, albeit 5 years later, the AABB board of directors charged a Babesia Policy Working Group to use the risk-based decision-making framework to recommend screening donors for Babesia microti.19 Prospects on the cost-effectiveness front are, however, not as promising. This is despite the fact that a recent comprehensive review of the sustainability of the United States blood supply focused on a number of reasons for the financial constraints faced by blood programs.20 The review had been developed by the RAND Corporation at the behest of the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health, Department of Health and Human Services, and it included an appraisal of the best practices in national blood programs elsewhere, many of which regard cost-effectiveness analyses as important considerations in determining blood center services. Although the report's authors suggested “robust conversation, to help guide health and human service policy makers,” any evidence for such a dialogue is elusive. The comments of Custer and Hoch in 2009, “it is hard to understand why the results of economic analyses are ignored” are just as appropriate today.21 Without wanting to impose a biblical tone on this commentary, it is worth reflecting on our profession's ability to, at best, delay attention to our prophets, or, at worst, ignore them. It was 25 years ago that Isbister wrote about the importance of physicians “avoiding allogeneic transfusion whenever possible,” thereby ushering in what was subsequently recognized as patient blood management.22 Zou and colleagues wrote about the aging of the donor base 15 years ago.23 It was also 15 years ago that a paper from the State Key Laboratory of Emerging Infectious Diseases at the University of Hong Kong warned “the possibility of the reemergence of SARS and other novel viruses from animals or laboratories and therefore the need for preparedness should not be ignored.”24 So many of our publications end with “more research is needed.” That is all well and good, but with previously identified challenges unaddressed, a better proposition could be “more attention to unresolved issues is needed.” The author has disclosed no conflicts of interest.

title: CytoDINO: Risk-Aware and Biologically-Informed Adaptation of DINOv3 for Bone Marrow Cytomorphology
authors: Aziz Muminov; Anne Pham
abstract: Bone marrow cell cytomorphology analysis is critical for the diagnosis of hematological malignancies but remains a labor-intensive process subject to significant inter-observer variability. While recent foundation models have shown promise in computational pathology, they often require extensive computational resources and fail to account for the asymmetric risks associated with clinical misdiagnosis. We introduce CytoDINO, a framework that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Munich Leukemia Laboratory (MLL) dataset by fine-tuning DINOv3 using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Our primary contribution is a novel Hierarchical Focal Loss with Critical Penalties, which encodes biological relationships between cell lineages and explicitly penalizes clinically dangerous misclassifications (e.g., classifying blasts as normal cells). CytoDINO achieves an 88.2% weighted F1 score and 76.5% macro F1 on a held-out test set of 21 cell classes. By utilizing parameter-efficient fine-tuning with only 8% trainable parameters on a single NVIDIA RTX 5080, we demonstrate that consumer-grade hardware can match specialized infrastructure. Furthermore, confidence-based selective prediction yields 99.5% accuracy on 67% of samples, suggesting a viable pathway for clinical deployment where high-uncertainty cases are flagged for expert review

title: The Endogeneity Paradox and Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Systems Review of Dochkina (2026)
authors: Syed Muntasir Mamun
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Dochkina (2026) presents the largest systematic computational experiment to date (≈25,000 task runs across 20,810 configurations) examining coordination architectures in multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems. The central claim is the endogeneity paradox: a hybrid protocol (Sequential) that fixes agent ordering exogenously while allowing fully endogenous role selection and participation outperforms both fully centralized (Coordinator, +14%, p < 0.001) and fully autonomous (Shared, +44%, Cohen's d = 1.86, p < 0.0001) designs. The study demonstrates sub-linear scaling to 256 agents (p = 0.61), emergent phenomena (dynamic role invention with RSI → 0, voluntary self-abstention, shallow hierarchies), and a capability threshold below which self-organization reverses. This review provides a deep mechanistic/architectural dissection of the proposed protocols and emergent dynamics, evaluates strengths and limitations, contrasts findings with leading multi-agent LLM research, and analyses the paper's underlying ontology and epistemology. While the experimental scale Mamun, SM (2026)………………………………1 A Critical Architectural Review of Self-Organizing LLM Agents: The Endogeneity Paradox and Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Systems Review of Dochkina (2026) and discovery of the endogeneity paradox constitute major contributions, reliance on LLM-as-judge evaluation and synthetic tasks limits external validity. Also available on Academia.edu: https://www.academia.edu/attachments/132416001/download_file?s=portfolio

title: An auditable conditional-strategy framework for open-ended decision-making in complex lung cancer
authors: Daoyun Wang; Zhicheng Huang; Huaiyuan Sun; Jiaqi Xu; Xiaowei Xu; Zhibo Zheng; Zhongxing Bing; Yuxiao Lin; Yicheng Liang; Chao Gao; Bowen Xue; Kai Zhang; Song Xu; Yan Wanpu; Hui Xia; Lin Li; Xiang Yan; Mu Hu; Qianli Ma; 薛志强; Xiaofang Liu; 韩志海; Nan Zhang; 汤传昊; Tongmei Zhang; Lan Song; Zhaohui Zhu; Xuan Zeng; Shafei Wu; Hui Guan; Lei Deng; Huaxia Yang; Zeliang Lian; Wubin Sun; Yongxin Wang; Xiaohui Shen; Binlin Wang; Tiantian Gu; Yu Cui; Li Zhang; Shirui Wang; Nan Liang
abstract: Complex lung cancer decisions can involve several defensible pathways whose eligibility, sequencing and safety depend on unresolved information. Effective support must make explicit how patient conditions govern pathway eligibility, deferral and redirection. MedGPT Clinical Explorer (MCE) organizes alternatives, decision-changing unknowns, safety constraints and fallback into a conditional strategy for clinician review. To evaluate this representation in physician-authored strategies, multidisciplinary experts established case-specific references for 40 cases within a purposive 100-case corpus, and 250 physicians from 98 institutions produced 2,250 strategies under unaided, retrieval-reference and MCE-assisted conditions. MCE-assisted strategies expressed more applicable clinical requirements, measured by the Admissible Pathway Attainment Score (APAS; 0-100), than unaided strategies (adjusted difference, 12.87; 95% CI, 11.18-14.55) and retrieval-reference strategies (5.22; 3.52-6.93). With the same knowledge base available in the retrieval-reference and MCE-assisted conditions, the additional content centered on candidate pathways, decision-critical information and safety constraints. Physicians' whole-strategy acceptability judgments correlated with APAS (Spearman's rho = 0.671), while a complementary relationship audit assessed whether candidates, conditions and subsequent actions were coherently connected. Together, these findings identify two complementary dimensions of open-ended decision support: coverage of clinically relevant content and coherent links among pathways, conditions and subsequent actions. MCE provides a shared decision object that makes consequential omissions and pathway contingencies visible before action; prospective studies should evaluate its effects on clinical workflow and patient outcomes.

title: 중년 여성의 대학학습경험에서 나타난 자기형성과정 : 해석학적 근거이론을 중심으로
authors: Eun-Jin Kim; Seung-Hee Kang
venue: Korean Association for Adult and Continuing Education
abstract: The purpose of this study was to deeply understand and develop a substantive theory on the process of self-formation through the university learning experiences of middle-aged women(aged 45-65) who had experienced interruptions in their education in the past, using Rennie's hermeneutic grounded theory methodology. Ten middle-aged female university students from a regional national university participated in this study. The analysis of these interview data resulted in 121 meaning units, 33 subcategories, and 10 higher categories, which were interpreted as thematic categories. A process analysis was conducted to examine the trajectory of the learning experiences of middle-aged women over time. As a result, the process was analyzed into 7 stages: Deferral, Choice, Discovery, Confrontation, Connection, Growth, and Formation. However, during the transition from the Connection stage to the Growth stage, the unexpected obstacles of the COVID-19 pandemic emerged. Additionally, during the transition from the Growth stage to the Formation stage, unestablished learner identity and the lack of an integrated self-identity were identified as obstacles. The results of this study indicated that the self-formation of the participants is constructed within the context of relationships, where individuals scruntinize, deconstruct, and reconstruct themselves through their experiences of learning.

title: Falsifiable Release Gates for Self-Improving Systems: Standing Invariants at Scale
authors: Deepak Soni
abstract: Safety claims for self-improving agent runtimes are almost always self-graded: a policy file, a guardrail, a promise in a README. We describe falsifiable release gates, a methodology in which every new capability must pass a pre-declared, machine-checkable acceptance suite before it ships, while a fixed set of standing invariants is preserved across every gate. We instantiate it in Antahkarana, an open runtime, then do what a method paper is only vindicated by: we follow the same runtime as it grows and ask whether the guarantees survive. The safety-critical property, that no action reaches an effector without a capability token minted by a control ring, is machine-checked exhaustively over the reachable states of a bounded model; a deliberately broken model yields the shortest counterexample, so the checker demonstrably has teeth. We then carry the runtime through six further releases. Across every one, the action-safety invariants INV-1 through INV-6 held without a single change, and one release added three capabilities while introducing no new invariant. Under the same teeth discipline, six more machine-checked families were added: memory with provable unlearning, a governed agent, calibrated abstention over a post-quantum record, a harness of many sub-agents, the self-improvement loop itself, and the residency of what it produces. The acceptance suite grew from 122 tests to 563. The load-bearing result sits in the negative space: across more than a doubling of capability, the safety core was neither weakened nor redesigned. The last families are the first on real hardware: gated self-improvement compounds a small model from 20% to 70% accuracy while auto-rejecting a candidate that only inflates confidence, and the whole governed path costs 0.021 ms per request, 0.008% of model inference. We release the runtime, tools, and gate suite; every number reproduces with a single command.

title: AgroChat: A Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Assistant with Reliability-Aware Inference for Crop Diagnosis
authors: M Deepika; Pammi Rishita; Uppala Sreehitha; Pabba Vitesh Kumar; Soma Harsha Vardhan; Saraf Brinda
venue: International Conference on Innovative Mechanisms for Industry Applications
abstract: Agriculture faces many challenges such as crop diseases, pests, and changing weather conditions. However, many farmers in rural areas still find it difficult to get proper guidance because internet access is limited and expert support is expensive. Most existing tools give general advice and do not consider local environmental conditions. For example, they may suggest spraying chemicals just before rainfall, which reduces its effectiveness. To address these limitations, we propose AgroChat, an offline-first multimodal agricultural assistant designed for lowconnectivity environments. Unlike a generic combination of CNN-based classification, retrieval-augmented generation, and languagemodel reasoning, AgroChat combines dual visual diagnosis branches for plant disease and insect recognition, retrieval-grounded advisory generation from a curated agricultural knowledge base, optional weather-aware conditioning, and a reliability-aware abstention mechanism that withholds responses when supporting evidence is insufficient. The system uses two EfficientNet-B0 classifiers, ChromaDB retrieval with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, and a locally deployed LLaMA 3.2 1B model to generate grounded recommendations without cloud dependency. Our results show that the system achieves 91.2% response accuracy with a hallucination rate of 8.6%, demonstrating its ability to provide reliable and context-aware agricultural decision support for farmers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/Sreehitha05/Agrochat.git.

title: Trustworthy machine learning methods for the analysis of polysomnographies
authors: Dries Van der Plas
abstract: Machine Learning (ML) is widely applied to automate repetitive tasks, offering potential benefits across various domains. These include safety-sensitive applications such as the analysis of polysomnographies in sleep medicine. Although there are unmistakably many benefits of using machine learning for sleep analyses, concerns have been raised about the accuracy and robustness of the proposed models. This prevents the models from being integrated in the medical routines. We draw inspiration from concrete challenges posed by two applications in sleep analysis: sleep stage scoring and respiratory analysis. We propose multiple machine learning approaches for enhancing the trustworthiness and reliability of ML models. Moreover, we illustrate their efficacy on the two aforementioned medical tasks. We focus on three different aspects: the explainability of the model, the ambiguity of labels and predictions, and the robustness of the model. The primary barrier is the lack of explainability of the developed models that leads medical experts to be cautious about incorporating new learned models into their workflows. Because medical experts retain ultimate responsibility for care, even when models are accurate and time-saving, the lack of transparency (e.g., about what data was used to train the model, how it arrives at its prediction) still represents a significant hurdle. We address this concern in sleep stage scoring by proposing a classifier which mimics the way humans score which makes it simple to explain. Furthermore, we developed a novel method for multiple sequence alignment on sequences of item sets. This enables identifying pathological breathing patterns such as apnea and hypopnea without the need for complicated feature construction or classification methods. The second barrier is the ambiguity of the class labels in the data. Despite having access to a sufficiently large training set, an ML model can still make systematic mistakes. For some observations, it may, for example, not be possible to unambiguously associate a single class label such as for observations in a transition region between two classes. Moreover, the training data can contain too many incorrectly labeled examples. This ambiguity has two consequences which we tackle. First, there are examples for which the model is not able to predict a single class with high certainty. We resolve this by introducing a reject option into the sleep stage classifier, i.e., we allow the classifier to abstain from predicting a sleep stage if it is too uncertain in its prediction. Second, it is not possible to evaluate the model using standard techniques when the true class label for a test example is not unique. Hence, we developed an alternative performance evaluation that takes both the prediction and label uncertainty into account. The third barrier is the lack of robustness present in ML models when they are forced to extrapolate to regions of the feature space that were not (sufficiently) present in the training data. Such extrapolation is omnipresent in many practical cases in which a model is (unintentionally) used on data that deviates from the training set. In sleep medicine, for example, the data is affected by factors such as the patient’s age, gender and pathologies. Hence, it is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to ensure that the training data is sufficiently diverse and exhaustive. We show that an anomaly detector is useful to identify deviating patients in sleep stage scoring. However, this approach results in a sub-optimal rejection performance when applied on individual predictions, i.e., the reject option is often too aggressive in practice as there are many seemingly anomalous patterns which are easy to classify accurately. This is, for example, the case when a patient is moving. In that case, multiple sensors register signals with very high and unique amplitudes while movement is often associated with wakefulness. Therefore, we introduce a new two-step rejection framework which includes a dependency between the reject option and the classifier itself to overcome this problem.

title: RigorBench: Benchmarking Engineering Process Discipline in Autonomous AI Coding Agents
authors: Meher Bhaskar Madiraju; Meher Sai Preetam Madiraju
abstract: Agentic coding harnesses - such as Agent-Skills, Superpowers, and Agent-Rigor - are increasingly deployed to augment underlying LLMs for real-world software engineering tasks. Existing benchmarks evaluate these agents almost exclusively on outcome correctness: whether generated code passes tests or resolves issues. We argue that this outcome-only lens is insufficient: an agent that arrives at a correct solution through reckless trial-and-error, without planning, verification, or graceful recovery, is fundamentally less reliable than one that follows sound engineering discipline. We introduce RigorBench, the first benchmark designed to measure process discipline in AI coding agents. RigorBench evaluates these harnesses across five pillars: Planning Fidelity, Verification Coverage, Recovery Efficiency, Abstention Quality, and Atomic Transition Integrity. A composite RigorScore aggregates these dimensions into a single metric via a weighted sum. We curate a suite of 30 tasks spanning five categories - Plan-Then-Build, Verify-Or-Die, Doom Loop Gauntlet, Know When to Fold, and Don't Break the Build-and evaluate leading harnesses in a controlled with/without experimental design against baseline coding assistants. Our results show that structured process discipline not only improves process quality scores by an average of 41% but also raises downstream outcome correctness by 17%, providing the first quantitative evidence that how agents code matters as much as what they produce. We release the full benchmark, scoring rubrics, and trajectory analysis tools as open-source artifacts.

title: A 149M Text Encoder as the First Tier for Phone Agents: Pre-Registered Routing to Frontier Models
authors: Chaitanya Talapalli
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Phone agents send every step to a frontier model, although many steps are easy. We ask whether Milo Pointer, a 149M-parameter text encoder that reads the screen's accessibility tree, can answer the steps it is confident about and defer the rest, offline on AndroidControl with a human-written instruction for each step. Each registered hypothesis, with its threshold and sample, was fixed in a dated log before any frontier model saw its steps. The small model answers 71-75% of steps on the device. Routing the rest to Claude Opus 5.5, given 16 retrieved training examples, is non-inferior to Opus alone in every registered comparison at under a third of its cost, and beat it in a registered confirmatory test with either deferral rule (+2.2 to +2.8 points, p <= 0.02). Pooled over 1,650 test steps the gain is 1.5 points ([+0.5, +2.4]; 1.1 on corrected labels), although the small model alone is not better than Opus: the two models err on different steps. Routing to Claude Sonnet 5.5 lifts Sonnet by 2.4-2.7 points. Alone, the text-only model scores 86.1% on AndroidControl-Low under the screenshot-agent protocol, above the 85.2% reported for OS-Atlas-7B on a slightly different step set. In a registered test with Claude Haiku 5.5 on fresh in-domain steps, a fallback shown only the small model's five best elements matched the full screen at half the input. A retrain that never used the test split reproduces the small model's accuracy. The evidence covers single steps: a related cascade lost on live multi-step tasks. We release the model, every system's per-step outputs and the registration log.

title: Defining the Clinical Indication for Real‐Time Artificial Intelligence–Assisted Ultrasound in Breast Lesions with Low Suspicion of Malignancy
authors: Jeeyeon Lee; Bora Yang; Won Hwa Kim; Jaeil Kim; Ho Yong Park; Byeongju Kang; Joon Suk Moon; HAI LIN PARK
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether real-time artificial intelligence (AI) breast ultrasound (US) can identify a subgroup of breast imaging reporting and data system (BI-RADS) category 4A lesions without suspicious mammographic (MMG) findings in whom unnecessary biopsy may be safely avoided. METHODS: This retrospective analysis of single-center biopsy registry included 641 consecutive US BI-RADS 4A lesions that underwent vacuum-assisted breast biopsy. Before conducting biopsy, the lesions were reassessed using a real-time AI US system (CadAI-B®), and MMG findings were classified as suspicious or non-suspicious based on formal reports. Seven prespecified biopsy-decision strategies were evaluated, including 3 AI-only strategies, 3 mammography-gated AI strategies, and the current standard strategy of biopsy all BI-RADS 4A lesions. The primary outcomes were biopsy reduction rate, missed cancers, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and accuracy, with final pathology as the reference standard. RESULTS: Among 641 cases of US BI-RADS 4A lesions, 26 cases of malignancies (4.1%) were identified, including 14 cases of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), 11 cases of invasive ductal carcinomas, and 1 case of apocrine carcinoma. AI reassigned 289 cases of lesions (45.1%) to BI-RADS categories 1-3. AI-only biopsy-deferral strategies missed 30.8% and 38.5% of malignancies when biopsy was deferred for AI BI-RADS ≤2 and ≤3 lesions, respectively, with DCIS accounting for most missed cancers. In contrast, among lesions without suspicious MMG findings, no malignancies were observed in AI BI-RADS 1-3 lesions. The sequential strategy of deferring biopsy only for lesions with AI BI-RADS ≤3 and non-suspicious MMG findings reduced biopsies by 43.5% (279/641) while maintaining 100.0% sensitivity (95% CI, 87.1-100.0%) and increasing specificity to 45.4% (95% CI, 41.4-49.4%). CONCLUSION: Real-time AI breast US alone could not safely support biopsy deferral in US BI-RADS 4A lesions. However, after suspicious MMG findings had been excluded, AI identified a low-risk subgroup in whom unnecessary biopsy could be substantially reduced without compromising cancer detection. These findings suggest that the clinical utility of real-time AI breast US lies in patients without suspicious MMG findings. Prospective multicenter validation is warranted before clinical implementation.

title: Clinical Outcomes of Deferred Lesions by IVUS Versus FFR-Guided Treatment Decision
authors: Joo Myung Lee; Hangyul Kim; David Hong; Doyeon Hwang; Jinlong Zhang; Xinyang Hu; Jun Jiang; Chang‐Wook Nam; Joon‐Hyung Doh; Bong‐Ki Lee; Weon Kim; Jinyu Huang; Fan Jiang; Hao Zhou; Peng Chen; Lijiang Tang; Wenbing Jiang; Xiaomin Chen; Wenming He; Jeehoon Kang; Sung Gyun Ahn; Myeong‐Ho Yoon; Ung Kim; You‐Jeong Ki; Eun‐Seok Shin; Ki Hong Choi; Taek Kyu Park; Jeong Hoon Yang; Young Bin Song; Seung‐Hyuk Choi; Hyeon‐Cheol Gwon; Bon‐Kwon Koo; Hyo-Soo Kim; Seung‐Jea Tahk; Jianan Wang; Joo‐Yong Hahn; the FLAVOUR Investigators
abstract: BACKGROUND: There are limited data regarding the safety of deferral of percutaneous coronary intervention based on intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) findings. The current study sought to compare the prognosis between deferred lesions based on IVUS and fractional flow reserve (FFR)–guided treatment decision. METHODS: This study is a post hoc analysis of the FLAVOUR randomized trial (Fractional Flow Reserve and Intravascular Ultrasound for Clinical Outcomes in Patients With Intermediate Stenosis) that compared 2-year clinical outcomes between IVUS- and FFR-guided treatment decision on intermediate coronary artery lesions using predefined criteria. In both IVUS and FFR groups, vessels were classified into deferred or revascularized vessels, and patients were classified as those with or without deferred lesions. Vessel-oriented composite outcomes (cardiac death, target vessel myocardial infarction, or target vessel revascularization) in deferred vessels and patient-oriented composite outcomes (death, myocardial infarction, or any revascularization) in patients with deferred lesions were compared between the IVUS and FFR groups. RESULTS: A total of 1682 patients and 1820 vessels were analyzed, of which 922 patients and 989 vessels were deferred. At 2 years, there was no difference in the cumulative incidence of vessel-oriented composite outcomes in deferred vessels between IVUS (n=375) and FFR (n=614) groups (3.8% versus 4.1%; hazard ratio, 0.91 [95% CI, 0.47–1.75]; P =0.77). The risk of vessel-oriented composite outcomes was comparable between deferred and revascularized vessels following treatment decision by IVUS (3.8% versus 3.5%; hazard ratio, 1.09 [95% CI, 0.54–2.19]; P =0.81) and FFR (4.1% versus 3.6%; hazard ratio, 1.14 [95% CI, 0.56–2.32]; P =0.72). In comparison of patient-oriented composite outcomes in patients with deferred lesions, there was no significant difference between the IVUS (n=357) and FFR (n=565) groups (6.2% versus 5.9%; hazard ratio, 1.05 [95% CI, 0.61–1.80]; P =0.86). CONCLUSIONS: In patients with intermediate coronary artery stenosis, deferral of percutaneous coronary intervention based on IVUS-guided treatment decision showed comparable risk of clinical events with FFR-guided treatment decision. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT02673424.

title: Do AI dream of P and S picks? Multimodal LLMs applied to visual seismological analysis
authors: Raffaele Di Stefano; Valentino Lauciani; Fabrizio Bernardi; Daniele Bailo; Maddalena Michele; Maria Grazia Ciaccio; Simone Marzorati
abstract: Abstract While conventional deep learning pipelines excel at high-throughput seismic processing, they often reduce complex perceptual tasks to rigid numerical matrices, lacking the contextual visual reasoning inherent to human experts. This study introduces an advanced proof-of-concept demonstrating the novel application of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to visual seismological analysis, proving that multimodal generative AI can replicate expert visual heuristics to enable boosted human-like scientific interpretation. We engineered an adaptive, multi-stage foveated vision framework that dynamically rescales high-resolution, lossless waveform graphics to optimize spatial pattern recognition within the model's vision encoder. To mitigate attention saturation, we developed a streamlined, Markdown-scaffolded prompt system. Furthermore, forensic examination of VLM outputs exposed critical operational failure modes—specifically compliance bias and text-scalar decoupling—leading us to propose a conceptual two-tier framework featuring a morphological abstention protocol designed to safely reject corrupted signals. Containerized into an unattended machine-to-machine orchestrator, the automated pipeline confirms that input image fidelity and structured visual scaling are decisive for millisecond-level pattern extraction. Finally, comparative benchmarks with self-hosted open-weight architectures demonstrate the concrete feasibility of local, in-house deployments, laying the foundation for transparent, reproducible, and institutionally sovereign AI ecosystems in operational geosciences.

title: A semi-automated software program to assess the impact of second reads in prostate MRI for equivocal lesions: results from a UK tertiary referral centre
authors: Alexandre Woernle; Louise Dickinson; Steven Lelie; Douglas A. Pendsé; Daniel Heffernan Ho; Navin Ramachandran; Alex P. S. Kirkham; Conrad Brice von Stempel; Shonit Punwani; Chun Wah So; John Withington; Alistair Grey; Thomas Collins; Davide Maffei; Aiman Haider; Alex Freeman; Mark Emberton; Jonathan W. Piper; Caroline M. Moore; John E.W. Hines; Clément Orczyk; Clare Allen; Francesco Giganti
abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate the utility of a prostate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) second read using a semi-automated software program in the one-stop clinic, where patients undergo multiparametric MRI, review and biopsy planning in one visit. We looked at concordance between readers for patients with equivocal scans and the possibility for biopsy deferral in this group. METHODS: We present data from 664 consecutive patients. Scans were reported by seven different expert genitourinary radiologists using dedicated software (MIM®) and a Likert scale. All scans were rescored by another expert genitourinary radiologist using a customised workflow for second reads that includes annotated biopsy contours for accurate visual targeting. The number of scans in which a biopsy could have been deferred using biopsy results and prostate specific antigen density was assessed. Gleason score ≥ 3 + 4 was considered clinically significant disease. Concordance between first and second reads for equivocal scans (Likert 3) was evaluated. RESULTS: A total of 209/664 (31%) patients scored Likert 3 on first read, 128 of which (61%) were concordant after second read. 103/209 (49%) of patients with Likert 3 scans were biopsied, with clinically significant disease in 31 (30%) cases. Considering Likert 3 scans that were both downgraded and biopsied using the workflow-generated biopsy contours, 25/103 (24%) biopsies could have been deferred. CONCLUSIONS: Implementing a semi-automated workflow for accurate lesion contouring and targeting biopsies is helpful during the one-stop clinic. We observed a reduction of indeterminate scans after second reading and almost a quarter of biopsies could have been deferred, reducing the potential biopsy-related side effects.

title: Nonlinear and Vessel-Specific Association Between Coronary Artery Calcium Burden and Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography Underestimation of Coronary Stenosis
authors: Xuzhe Wang; Chengzhuo Wang; Yu Xie; Wenyu Wang; Ruifeng Liu
abstract: Background: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) introduces substantial artifacts in coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA). Although calcification is classically associated with overestimation of stenosis severity, underestimation may be even more clinically hazardous because underestimation can lead to inappropriate deferral of revascularization. Thus, this study aimed to investigate the association between CAC burden and CCTA underestimation, with emphasis on vessel-specific anatomical heterogeneity. Methods: We retrospectively evaluated 673 patients without known coronary artery disease who underwent both CCTA and invasive coronary angiography (ICA) within 90 days, yielding 2692 vessel observations. Underestimation was defined strictly at the vessel level as a CCTA stenosis grade lower than the corresponding ICA grade. Restricted cubic splines (RCS) were used to characterize the nonlinear association between CAC burden and the risk of underestimation. Within-patient clustering across the left main (LM), left anterior descending (LAD), left circumflex (LCX), and right coronary artery (RCA) was accounted for using generalized estimating equations (GEEs). Results: Any-vessel underestimation occurred in 389 patients (57.8%). Vessel-specific susceptibility varied markedly: LM, 3.0%; LAD, 27.9%; LCX, 29.3%; and RCA, 22.4%. RCS analysis demonstrated a significant nonlinear association between total CAC score and patient-level underestimation in the fully adjusted model (p-overall = 0.014; p-nonlinear = 0.004), with an upward risk trajectory observed as calcification increased relative to the median reference of 301. GEE modeling confirmed that patient-level CAC burden independently predicted vessel-level underestimation (CAC ≥400 vs. 0: odds ratio, 2.01; 95% confidence interval, 1.20–3.36; p = 0.008), with a significant interaction between CAC and vessel territory (p < 0.001). A sensitivity analysis restricted to patients without any CCTA overestimation (n = 155) confirmed a robust nonlinear association between total CAC score and pure underestimation risk (p-overall = 0.012; p-nonlinear = 0.005), suggesting that concurrent overestimation noise partially obscures this dynamic risk trajectory in the full cohort. Conclusions: The association between calcification burden and CCTA underestimation is nonlinear and strongly dependent on coronary territory. Since the RCS-derived odds ratio (OR) = 1, crossings depend on the median reference value (CAC = 301) and should be interpreted as markers of risk trajectory rather than absolute diagnostic cutoffs. Integrating total calcium burden with vessel-specific susceptibility may help mitigate the risk of missed severe stenosis on CCTA.

title: The 4C Dialysis Study: Centralization, Clinical Care, Choice, and Consequences in Advanced Kidney Disease - A Retrospective Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of Renal-System Policy and Dialysis Uptake, 2005-2025
authors: Albert Kadri
abstract: The 4C Dialysis Study is a retrospective longitudinal quasi-experimental evaluation of whether sequential changes in kidney-care guidance, health-system organization, primary-care referral pathways, multidisciplinary advanced-CKD eligibility, dialysis-deferral performance measurement, goals-of-care processes, conservative kidney management, funding, regional implementation, and the alignment of nephrology/renal-service capacity with changing population need were temporally associated with changes in dialysis uptake and clinically important renal outcomes. The study organizes exposures hierarchically at national (Canada), provincial (Ontario), and regional/local levels and evaluates both geographic adaptation of renal resources and capacity adaptation within existing centres. It uses within-Ontario comparisons, interrupted time-series methods, difference-in-differences/event-study approaches, competing-risk/time-to-event methods where patient-level data permit, and external Great Lakes and U.S. comparator jurisdictions where assumptions can be supported. The study is hypothesis-testing but neutral as to benefit or harm. Policy and organizational exposures will be ascertained across the study observation period, with outcomes evaluated through March 31, 2025. For exposures whose implementation dates remain uncertain, including dedicated conservative renal/kidney care funding, the definitive breakpoint will be assigned only after independent verification from contemporaneous policy, funding, or administrative documentation and before examination of definitive policy-effect estimates.

title: Evaluation du statut hydrique et du sommeil des athlètes durant le mois de Ramadan
authors: Khaled Trabelsi; Mohamed Romdhani; Juan-Jose Morillas Pedreno; Capucine Bertrand; Haitham Jahrami; Karim Chamari
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Ramadan fasting (RF) can induce hypohydration in athletes due to the abstention from water during daylight hours, as well as sleep disturbances related to modified training schedules and increased nighttime social activities. These changes may negatively affect athletic performance, making regular assessment of hydration and sleep essential. METHODS: This review is based on data from systematic reviews, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, narrative reviews, and expert consensus to provide practical recommendations tailored to the context of Ramadan. RESULTS: Body mass alone is not a reliable indicator for daily monitoring of hydration status due to changes in body composition during RF. Monitoring the specific gravity and color of the first morning urine sample is a simple, quick, and effective method. Pre- and post-exercise body mass measurement remains the most accurate approach for estimating acute fluid loss. For sleep monitoring, smartwatches and actigraphy are recommended. In the absence of these tools, sleep diaries may be used with caution. Standardized sleep questionnaires are not well-suited to the specific characteristics of Ramadan and should be avoided. Moreover, a state of hyperhydration may disrupt nighttime sleep by increasing nocturnal urination, highlighting the importance of simultaneously monitoring hydration status and sleep. CONCLUSION: Hydration status and sleep must be rigorously monitored throughout Ramadan to preserve overall health, reduce physiological strain, and optimize athletic performance.
