title: Blood bans and COVID-19: Government attempts to influence medicine and science threaten us all
authors: Jeremy W. Jacobs; Thomas C. Binns; David M. Chooljian; Brian D. Adkins; Jennifer S. Woo; Laura Dilly Stephens; Timothy D. Schlafer; Bipin N. Savani; Garrett S. Booth
abstract: Every 2 seconds someone in the United States needs blood or platelets. With nearly 16 million blood products transfused each year, blood transfusion is one of the most common medical procedures in the United States, contributing to life-saving medical care for millions annually.1 Despite the recent unparalleled blood shortages resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, the US health care system has largely managed to weather the potentially catastrophic situation of an inadequate blood supply, partially attributed to the development of COVID-19 vaccines blunting the pandemic and resulting demand. The result is maintenance of available blood for individuals with both emergent and nonemergent indications. On February 17, 2023, however, a state representative introduced Montana House Bill No. 645, which attempts to prohibit donation of blood from COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2)–vaccinated individuals.2 The bill also punishes individuals who “knowingly use, receive, accept, ship, transfer, or administer” blood from a COVID-19–vaccinated donor. Violations would result in a misdemeanor punishable by monetary penalty. This type of legislation would impose liability on numerous individuals—donors, patients, blood donation industry workers, health care professionals, etc. Although individuals refusing blood transfusion from COVID-19–vaccinated donors is not novel,3 this legislation seeks to validate unfounded, misinformed, and sometimes conspicuously prejudiced beliefs. We initially hesitated to address this effort with a formal response at the risk of conferring legitimacy, but we believe that such legislation threatens the very foundation of American health care so comprehensively that official condemnation is necessary. The evolution of COVID-19 vaccination skepticism has progressed from mere uncertainty to unsubstantiated medical ­misinformation and even intentional falsification. Vaccination misinformation has affected health care in a variety of settings,4 but threats to the US blood supply have prompted federal regulators to refute these claims.5 Maintaining the safety of the blood supply is a guiding principle in blood collection, and the lay public should be reassured that blood donors must be in good health at the time of donation. Donors must pass a health evaluation, including vital sign assessment, travel and contact history review, and extensive eligibility screening concerning pertinent therapies and illnesses. Every blood donation also undergoes testing for infectious agents that may be transmitted by blood. Further, the US blood donation system has existing deferral strategies for certain vaccinations, and vaccines are evaluated to determine whether donation deferral is necessary. Although no studies have been undertaken to directly assess the effect of transfusion from vaccinated blood donors on recipients, there is no historical or contemporary scientific basis to believe that this blood poses any risk. As the COVID-19 vaccines do not contain live virus, there is no evidence that they pose an infection risk to recipients of the donated blood. Further, there is no evidence—and no logical reasoning—to believe that these vaccines would alter the genetic material of the vaccinated individual or blood transfusion recipient. Thus, legislation pertaining to risk should not be made until such data are reviewed. Notably, as of February 23, 2023, 81.2% of the US population had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose.6 Although the exact proportion of COVID-19–vaccinated US blood donors is unknown, a June 2022 study demonstrated an increase in the seroprevalence rate in blood donors from 3.5% in July 2020 to 20.2% for SARS-CoV-2 infection–induced antibodies to 83.3% for combined SARS-CoV-2 infection– and vaccine-induced antibodies by May 2021, higher than the general population rate at that time.7 The combined seroprevalence increased further to 94.7% by December 2021, highlighting the significant uptake of at least 1 vaccine dose across the United States.7 Despite this finding, no adverse effects in recipients of blood transfusion from vaccinated donors attributable to the vaccine have been described to date. Further, as data have shown that blood donors tend to be vaccinated against COVID-19 at higher rates than the general public, these types of proposals could contribute to blood shortages in regions and jurisdictions in which the laws are enacted. Likewise, if additional states were to adopt such a restricted approach, these policies could pose a theoretical risk to the adequacy of the US blood supply on a larger scale. With no US Food and Drug Administration–approved blood substitute available, clinical outcomes in regions with a lack of blood availability would regress. Perhaps just as significantly, these proposals would prohibit research and emergency use authorization therapies essential for responding to and preventing pandemics, including those not directly involving vaccines. For instance, numerous hospitals used blood products containing SARS-CoV-2 infection–induced antibodies collected from blood donors previously infected with SARS-CoV-2 (ie, convalescent plasma) as a therapeutic strategy for COVID-19 before the advent of vaccines. Objections to the use of blood products from vaccinated donors may be related to the fact that such donations are not distinctly labeled to promote awareness and choice; however, if labeling were present, it would simply demonstrate that the majority of products are from vaccinated donors, without a valid clinical reason to do so and potentially inducing a chilling effect on both donation and receipt of such blood.7 Notwithstanding the ethical considerations of this practice, the financial and administrative burden for such unfounded implementation would further negatively affect the blood donation infrastructure. Unfortunately, the looming threat to patient care is not limited to Montana. Proposed Connecticut Senate Bill No. 531, introduced on January 18, 2023, would amend Connecticut law to “permit an individual the right to choose blood transfusion from an unvaccinated individual.”8 This bill presumes that the blood transfusion recipient, physician, or the hospital itself knows the blood donor’s vaccination status, which is not the case in the United States. Blood products are not labeled with the donor’s COVID-19 vaccination status because this information has no clinical impact on the transfusion recipient, similar to other individual characteristics, such as race and ethnicity. Essentially, this bill implies that a patient should be able to request a directed donation from a particular donor based on vaccination status. Although we acknowledge patients’ general rights of autonomy and therefore refusal of therapy, in the absence of another justification, such as a rare blood type, there is no evidence that blood from a directed donor is safer than standard volunteer blood. Further, social pressures associated with directed donations may compromise the reliability of the donor history questionnaire, a crucial risk-mitigation strategy.9 Although the proposed legislation in Montana has been tabled, hopefully ending any meaningful consideration, it is noteworthy that the subcommittee did not vote it down outright. The Connecticut legislation has been referred to the state’s Senate Joint Committee on Public Health and is pending action. We believe that elected officials should proceed with extreme caution before proposing bills that may have profound impacts on health care without medical or scientific evidence to support their claims. These legislative precedents could set the stage for an impending legal, medical, and ethical battle among lawmakers, health care professionals, and vaccine skeptics, with the safety and sufficiency of the blood supply in the balance.

title: Voting for Democracy’s Future: The Role of Future Collective (Dis)continuity in Shaping Democratic Participation Among Italian Citizens
authors: Federica Scarci; Matilde Tumino; Andrea Manunza; Alessia Valmori; Luca Cussigh
abstract: On June 2, 1946, following the end of fascism and the war, the votes of Italian men and, for the first time, of Italian women marked the beginning of a democratic Italy, founded on citizen participation. Today, 80 years later, democracy continues to be generally regarded as a positive and desirable value; however, its stability appears increasingly uncertain, in a climate described as “democratic anxiety” . In Italy, this picture of instability is accompanied by a rise in voter abstention; in the most recent general election of 2022, turnout stood at around 64%, the lowest figure in the history of the Republic . This is an extremely significant problem, as voting represents one of the fundamental tools through which citizens exercise democracy and ensure its continuity over time. Research suggests that voting reflects a form of collective action, associated with ingroup identification and perceived collective efficacy . At the same time, a vast body of literature has highlighted the role of national identity and social identification in sustaining political participation . In applications to political phenomena, social identity has often been treated as a monolithic construct, focusing primarily on the strength of identification with the national ingroup . Recent evidence, however, suggests a more multifaceted conception of national identity, one that also includes how the ingroup is consistently represented over time. The concept of perceived collective continuity reflects the tendency to perceive social groups and their values and traditions as entities that persist over time across the past, present, and future . When individuals perceive that national identity has continuity, they feel part of something that preceded them and will continue after them, experiencing a sense of stability and security . Conversely, when the group’s collective continuity is threatened physically or symbolically, collective angst – i.e., a concern for the ingroup’s future vitality – may emerge, motivating members to act to protect and strengthen it . Furthermore, most studies have focused on the perception of collective continuity (vs. discontinuity) with respect to the past, highlighting the role of collective nostalgia in predicting ingroup protection and outgroup rejection . Recent research, however, introduced the concept of future collective continuity, that is, the perception that the ingroup will maintain a consistent trajectory in the future, showing that envisioning strong future continuity of the national ingroup can reduce collective angst and prejudice toward immigrants, while increasing prosocial attitudes and collective action intentions, especially among those who identify most strongly with the ingroup . If the future continuity of the ingroup can reduce anxiety and perceived threats, then a future discontinuity of the ingroup could trigger collective angst and motivate members to protect it. Yet, this possibility has not been directly examined for political participation. Applying this reasoning, the present project proposes that a future discontinuity in Italy’s identity, represented by the loss of democracy, may increase the importance of voting as a means of protecting the continuity of the national ingroup . Since the future is perceived as more open to action than the past, imagining a possible future discontinuity could motivate action in the present, making voting a tool for preserving the country’s democratic continuity . Furthermore, this project extends this framework to citizens residing abroad, whose continued engagement with the political life of their country of origin depends not only on the strength of their national identification but also on how they perceive the nation and its continuity across time and space. Indeed, citizens residing abroad, who are often overlooked in studies on political participation, may exercise their right to vote in elections in their country of origin . In the Italian context, voting from abroad tends to have lower and more unstable participation rates compared to voting by residents in Italy . Therefore, examining the perceptions of Italians living abroad enables us to understand whether Italy’s democratic continuity is perceived as significant depending on the strength of their ties to the nation. Geographical distance could alter the way Italians living abroad perceive national identity and could mitigate the impact of a threat to the ingroup. Therefore, comparing Italians living in Italy with those living abroad allows us to test whether a future discontinuity in the national ingroup motivates political participation and voting when national belonging is experienced through geographical proximity or transnational distance.

title: Digital Water Metering: A Framework and Modelling Tool for Benefit Valuation
authors: Ian Monks
abstract: Understanding the touchpoints of water usage metering and how meter data is used in all business areas of water utilities, and in the everyday lives of customers, can lead to an appreciation of the scale of obtainable benefits of digital water metering (DWM). The absence of a systematic cataloguing of benefits, and the measurement of their value to a water utility and its customers, may explain the lack of acceptance of this technology among water utilities. Manual meter reading has been identified as inefficient and ineffective for most utility processes, other than periodic billing for which it too can be problematic. DWM substantially eliminates the walking of meter reading routes by meter readers. It delivers over 2000 readings per quarter (at hourly intervals) rather than just the one reading obtained by the meter reader. Special trips to the property, which are required to read the manual meter when the customer leaves, are also eliminated. Sometimes the customer is asked to read the meter when the water utility cannot. DWM is accurate and automatic whereas manual meter reading is subject to mis-reads and estimation when the meter cannot be accessed. In Australia, and many other parts of the developed world, few water utilities have switched to DWM completely and, in many others, only in particular circumstances, usually involving a lack of physical access or where access by meter readers would be inefficient. Where significant network issues or scarce water resources have existed, digital meters have improved the management of the network and allowed the deferral of network augmentation and the conservation of water. This doctoral research study aimed to address this lack of knowledge of DWM benefits by searching for and cataloguing the benefits, and by developing plausible measures that provide probabilistic ranges of outcomes of savings and changes to customer sentiment. The objectives were to find as many benefits as possible from across water utilities’ operations and among customer interactions with their water and wastewater service provider; to value those benefits, particularly the less-tangible benefits: and to develop a tool to model the value of benefits for water utilities. To identify the benefits, an extensive literature review of academic and industry reports was conducted. Interviews were conducted with several current and past staff of water utilities. The literature review was backed up by structured interviews with employees with specific expertise from a cross section of companies and representing various roles within those organisations. Customers were surveyed directly to identify their responses to the potential of digital metering. Qualitative and quantitative methods were applied to the expert opinions and customer survey responses to develop a valuation model that calculates savings and change in customer satisfaction levels. Other surveys were conducted to collect data from water utilities on specific issues. The valuation model was trialled in the field. The methods and findings are presented in the four journal papers that are included in this thesis. In all, 77 benefits of DWM were identified. These were categorised into a taxonomy based on who would benefit, (i.e., the water business, the customer or both water business or customer) as well as the business areas and sub-areas of those beneficiaries. A second taxonomy was developed that categorised benefits according to sustainability themes. Qualitative analysis of the expert opinions regarding the benefits exposed the range of opinions on the likelihood that benefits could be achieved and the extent of the benefit. While quantifying the savings of individual benefits, two contexts were identified (Cost of Water savings, and Charges and Operational Cost savings) and the need for flexibility to meet local expectations was observed. The customer survey revealed the potential change in levels of customer satisfaction from a current 5.8 (0 – 10 scale) to between 6.2 and 8.8, with a simple average of 7.6. Separate valuation methods within the model were developed for each context. A third valuation method was developed for measuring change in customer satisfaction over multiple years. The application of the model, using a large metropolitan water utility’s data, calculated savings outcomes that were consistent with the utility’s cost-benefit analysis and provided the utility with risk-based probabilistic ranges. DWM benefit savings were also viewed through a sustainability lens after being allocated to the different sustainability themes. The trial raised issues with the framing of business cases for DWM projects and which were then examined. Other findings were made during the study. The commonly used scale used in the Net Promoter Score classification of customers was observed to be inaccurate for relationship type surveys of water utilities, and a new scale was proposed. The potential of data analytics applied to hourly meter readings to answer questions on usage within residential properties was examined through a case study of a regional water utility. A model to optimise the sequencing of meter deployment to gain benefits early was proposed and a prototype model presented. Further, an opportunity for a capability model for intelligent metering was identified and a preliminary model was developed. The study also proposed that a longitudinal study of the uplift in customer satisfaction from the use of DWM be conducted, and that a non-monetary measure of the value of social equity be developed and applied to DWM project proposals.

abstract: JSON Consistency Repair v0.41.0 is a conservative JSON rectification engine designed to recover determinable syntax damage and repair semantic inconsistencies only when the available evidence identifies a justified correction. The software combines strict JSON parsing with bounded deterministic grammar and lexical recovery, exact constraint discovery, reversible minimal patches, strong fixed-point closure, provenance and authority controls, active falsification of discovered relations, symmetry-aware abstention, controllability and attainability checks, persistent OPEN obligations, targeted incremental recomputation, horizon/distributed-coherence checks, residual-information bounds, and blind-reconstruction verification. It supports single JSON documents, multi-document bundles, JSONL/NDJSON, and bounded-memory top-level-array streaming. Cross-field and cross-record relations include functional, arithmetic, temporal, sequential, schema, enum, identity, reference, aggregate, conservation, graph/state and migration constraints. Conflicting duplicate keys are deliberately refused unless an authority resolves the ambiguity. Version 0.41.0 introduces two execution profiles. full performs exhaustive analysis, global correction search, replay, proof-graph reconstruction and independent final certification. fast still scans all analyzer families but restricts expensive deep correction and falsification to unique local actionable cones; it explicitly reports FAST_SCAN_ONLY and does not masquerade as full certification. The frozen PASS041 verification records 462/462 regression tests passed, 600/600 adversarial stress cases, 73/73 valid Draft 2020-12 public schemas, zero false mutations in the PASS041 stress campaign, successful fresh-source and fresh-wheel checks, and byte-for-byte reproducible wheel/source builds. The syntax contract records 13/13 determinable targeted corruptions repaired and 1/1 conflicting duplicate-key ambiguity correctly refused. PASS is evidence- and contract-relative: it means that no unresolved violation remains under the currently certified relations. It is not a claim of inaccessible external ground truth. Comparative benchmarks and raw validation artifacts are included so that performance and scope can be evaluated independently. title: Design and test validation of a novel low-cost quartz window for reducing heat losses in concentrating solar power applications
authors: Shaun D. Sullivan; James B. Kesseli
abstract: Concentrating Solar Power (CSP) continues to see increased deployment with nearly 5 GW of CSP installed worldwide. CSP is particularly attractive as a renewable energy source given that the storage and recovery of absorbed heat may be accomplished using sensible, latent, or thermochemical systems; this enables cost-effective deferral and on-demand dispatch of electricity generated from CSP, addressing mismatches between power demand and solar availability.Power tower and dish-based CSP configurations, in which reflected solar energy is focused onto a single central target, can generate very high temperatures; this enables the use of supercritical steam cycles, air Brayton cycles, or supercritical carbon dioxide (sCO2) power cycles that produce electricity at higher efficiencies than can be achieved with photovoltaic (PV) or linear-focus trough-based CSP systems. Critical to the performance and economics of all CSP systems is their ability to retain as much of the captured solar energy as possible. Heat losses to the environment directly penalize the efficiency of the system, requiring additional collector area to achieve the target power. The receiver, through which solar energy is absorbed and conveyed as heat into a working fluid, is necessarily the highest-temperature component in the system; as a result it has the greatest potential to lose heat via radiation to the environment. Furthermore, convection losses from the high temperature absorber to the ambient environment may also be high.Historically quartz windows have been employed in conjunction with cavity-type receivers, which are suitable for dish- mounted and small-scale power tower applications. Quartz is naturally transparent to wavelengths of visible light but is opaque to a large fraction of infrared wavelengths. Consequently, concentrated solar energy passes through a quartz surface unimpeded, but a significant fraction of the infrared radiation that might otherwise be lost from the hot absorber surface to the environment is absorbed by the window; this provides a radiation shield and reduces heat losses. The window may also impede the formation of convection cells, further reducing heat losses. These benefits must be weighed against the penalties imposed by the inclusion of a quartz window. For example, for every window surface that incoming light passes through at greater than its critical angle, there is a 4% reflection loss; this corresponds to a total energy loss of 7.8% in the case of a standard planar window, accounting for reflection losses at both front and back faces. Therefore the window is only practical if reduces heat losses by at least this amount. Furthermore, the cost of incorporating a quartz windows can be prohibitive, particularly in larger sizes (corresponding to larger power ratings and/or non-cavity receivers), more complex forms designed to reduce reflection losses, and for systems in which the window must react elevated internal pressures.To address these shortcomings Brayton Energy has developed, analyzed, and tested a novel quartz tube window system. This configuration employs commodity-priced thin-walled quartz tubes with L/D ratios of 3 or more. These tubes are arrayed in a close-packed configuration and mounted over the receiver aperture. Incoming concentrated sunlight only encounters thin tube wall surfaces at an angle exceeding the critical angle; consequently, the fraction of the aperture that is subject to the 4% reflection loss is very small. All other surface encounters occur along the lateral surface of the tube walls at an incident angle below the critical angle, resulting in reflections that redirect the light deeper into the cavity as opposed to back out to environment. Depending upon the specific receiver and absorber element configuration, a quartz-tube window design may be also implemented such that it impedes convection cells; this can further reduce heat losses to the environment and improve overall system efficiency.The design, analysis, fabrication, installation, and performance testing of quartz tube windows for two different receiver configurations will be reported here. These studies indicate that for the receiver applications studied, inclusion of a quartz tube window has the potential to dramatically reduce the thermal losses at the design point. Validation testing was performed to directly measure heat loss from systems at operating temperatures appropriate for a sCO2 power block both with and without the quartz tube window in place. Inclusion of a quartz tube window to the cavity receiver decreased its design point heat loss by up to 33%, depending on the receiver tilt angle. The addition of a quartz tube window to an open receiver module decreased its combined radiative and convective heat losses by more than 50%.

title: Chronic aortic dissection type A: simply an overlooked acute event?
authors: Sven Peterß; Christian M. Hagl; Maximilian Andreas Pichlmaier
abstract: The temporal categorization of aortic dissections is largely governed by mortality rates. Thus, mortality drops with time in the natural course of the disease as well as in the treatment thereof. While early papers simply distinguished between an ‘acute’ and a ‘chronic’ stage pivoting around day 14 after the onset of symptoms [1], more recent studies and expert consensus specify more concrete time periods. Booher et al. [2] analysed the survival according to localization of the entry and treatment strategy from the IRAD registry and identified the following time periods: 0–24 h (hyperacute), 2–7 days (acute), 8–30 days (subacute) and greater than 30 days (chronic). Accordingly, survival continuously drops towards the subacute and chronic stages, while mortality remains high in the acute stages regardless of the treatment strategy. The 2014 ESC Guidelines defined 3 stages: acute 90 days [3]. The survival-based categories also have mechanical and histopathological correlates [4]. Aortic enlargement and thus the aortic growth rate changes during the transition from acute to chronic stages. The rapid enlargement seen early on may thus reflect the virulence of the disease within the hyperacute and acute stages, whereas the decelerated expansion in the subacute and chronic stages indicates clinical stability. The increase in flap thickness/stiffness and lost amplitude of mobility are other accepted indicators of the chronic stage. Histopathological examinations have shown time-dependent elastin fragmentation and fibrosis of the media. Whereas the transition from acute to chronic aortic dissection favours the outcome of open repair, endovascular treatment may actually lose efficacy with time, while also carrying a higher procedural risk at the very early stages of the disease. Wu et al. [5] published in this issue of the journal the surgical results of 181 patients with newly diagnosed subacute and chronic (>14 days) aortic dissections type A and compared them to 911 acute cases. They found a significantly better outcome compared to acute stages ( 90%) in both groups received total arch replacements—and the unilateral cerebral perfusion technique used. Even the ‘acute’ cases were treated on average 1.2 days after the onset of symptoms and, consequently, were strictly speaking not operated on in the hyperacute stage. Their results are generally in agreement with other groups. Rylski et al. [6], for example, also reported improved mortality (4.5 vs 13.2%) and 5-year survival (80 vs 68%) in chronic cases. The better outcome of surgery in the chronic stage may be the result of the above-mentioned settlement of the active and adverse anatomical and histopathological processes. The increased fibrosis in the media and the deceleration of remodelling over time simplify the technical aspects of the procedure. Secondly, natural selection has taken away the sicker patients and thus positively impacts on survival. However, even if delayed surgical intervention appears opportunistic from various standpoints, the disproportionately high mortality of the natural course within the hyperacute, acute and even early subacute stages makes deliberate deferral of the surgical procedure irresponsible in most cases [1, 2]. Thus, guidelines clearly recommend prompt and urgent surgical treatment [3]. Therefore, chronic aortic dissections type A are generally a rare and highly elusive entity. They remain undetected in the acute stage because the patient expires, the event occurs during cardiac surgery or the disease truly remains asymptomatic [5–7]. Possible further explanations may be that the extent of dissection is more often limited (e.g. DeBakey Type II), malperfusion is observed less frequently, and scattered geographical distribution of aortic centres like those in China handicaps correct and prompt diagnosis and treatment [4–6]. Thus, the comparison of the risk of operative treatment of acute and chronic dissection type A must be drawn with care as the patient cohorts clearly differ.

title: 17 — Limitations, Scope Conditions, and Refusal Criteria
authors: Kenneth Lee Roberts
abstract: # 17 — Refusal, Retained Roles, and Reconsideration This component defines how the Space Bioindustrial Architecture conditions, defers, assigns horizon status to, quarantines, refuses, retires, narrows, or reopens exact settlement-infrastructure claims. Its governing principle is: > **Refusal is claim control, not technology dismissal.** A credible settlement-readiness architecture must be able to say that a claim is not yet supported, supported only under stated conditions, relevant only to a later stage, temporarily suspended pending investigation, unsupported for the present case, unsupported for the present package version, unsupported for the declared use class or environment, unsupported as accepted contribution, unsupported as avoided import, unsupported as baseline displacement, unsupported as autonomy, unsupported as terrestrial resilience, or unsupported as settlement readiness. The formal decision object is the **exact claim**, not the technology class as a whole. A claim may concern candidate admission, stage placement, accepted output, closure, avoided import, baseline displacement, operational readiness, interruption tolerance, autonomy, lifecycle-qualified contribution, biosafety, planetary protection, terrestrial transfer, resilience, or settlement readiness. The architecture applies the narrowest status that prevents overclaim while preserving what remains valid. Component 17 distinguishes the formal evaluated claim states: * **Countable** * **Conditional** * **Deferred** * **Horizon Item** * **Quarantined** * **Refused** * **Retired** These states must not be used interchangeably. Missing but plausibly obtainable evidence generally supports **Deferred** status rather than Refused status. Later-stage relevance supports **Horizon Item** status. Temporary safety, output-quality, configuration, evidence-integrity, cybersecurity, or registry uncertainty supports **Quarantined** status. Refusal is reserved for an exact claim that is unsupported, unsafe, incompatible, inappropriate, or misleading for the declared case and evidence state. The component groups limitation and refusal triggers into eight major families: requirement or profile failure; package or interface incompleteness; output or acceptance failure; burden or dependency failure; interruption or recovery failure; safety, biosafety, or planetary-protection failure; registry, software, evidence-integrity, or authority failure; and comparator, alternative, or profile-transfer failure. A key function of the component is to preserve legitimate retained roles after non-countable decisions. A refused infrastructure claim may still leave a valid role as a research candidate, experimental payload, analog test article, contained demonstration, hybrid augmentation plug-in, evidence-building system, future-stage item, design reference, comparator item, training platform, current-case rejection only, or historical record. Refusal controls the claim; it does not erase supported scientific, engineering, operational, terrestrial, or developmental value. Every limited or non-countable decision must also identify prohibited claims and exclusions. Depending on the decision, the package may not be represented as providing infrastructure credit, accepted-output credit, avoided import, baseline displacement, autonomy, lifecycle-positive contribution, medical use, food use, potable-water use, atmospheric use, surface validation, terrestrial resilience, disaster-proofing, unbounded sustainability, or settlement readiness. Component 17 links refusal and limitation decisions to the registry and to the Capability and Assurance Gap Register. Where further work remains plausible, a refusal, deferral, quarantine, or condition should identify the evidence, redesign, validation, acceptance, burden closure, dependency closure, authority action, or profile revision required for reconsideration. Gap closure permits renewed review; it does not automatically restore readiness or claim status. The component distinguishes two main reopening pathways. A claim that has not yet reached validation or authorization returns through evidence-gap closure, evidence-profile reassessment, exact-package verification and validation, downstream acceptance, comparator and burden review, evidence-sufficiency adjudication, and claim authorization. A claim that was previously validated or authorized but later affected by interruption, repair, anomaly, expiry, configuration change, or changed use returns through configuration verification, restart and stabilization where applicable, package and output revalidation, downstream reacceptance, burden and dependency reassessment, evidence readjudication, and claim reauthorization. PBR-001 demonstrates the doctrine. Prior art supported biological plausibility, photosynthetic CO₂ uptake, oxygen evolution, biomass production, terrestrial cultivation, modeling, limited spaceflight experimentation, lunar design analysis, and analog development. That evidence justified admission and continued development. It did not establish accepted oxygen, accepted biomass, avoided import, displaced baseline ECLSS function, complete package allocation, qualified atmosphere and output interfaces, qualified power and thermal integration, complete lifecycle burden, autonomous recovery and validation, downstream reacceptance after restart, or positive lifecycle-qualified infrastructure contribution. For the declared case, the supported values remained: accepted oxygen 0 kg, accepted biomass 0 kg, avoided import 0 kg, and displaced baseline function none. The infrastructure claim was therefore Refused, while a contained experimental or hybrid evidence-building role was retained. Component 17 therefore supplies the architecture’s disciplined negative-decision layer. It prevents promising technologies from being overclaimed, preserves valid retained roles, identifies prohibited claims, creates registry-visible reconsideration conditions, and defines the pathway by which better evidence, better packages, better interfaces, accepted outputs, burden closure, authority review, or changed claims may re-enter evaluation.

title: Pillar 20: The Story of How Cosmological Pangaea Unfolded
authors: Charles Richard Walker (C. Rich)
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Cosmological Pangaea: Decoding the Universe With Artificial Intelligence is a first-person scientific memoir in which an independent researcher in rural Georgia uses a “Pantheon” of AI systems to audit modern cosmology with a brutally enforced Occam’s razor. Starting from frustration with the “ninety-five percent unknown” of dark matter, dark energy, and inflation, he builds a GR-respecting demolition program (the GR-Razor Stress Tests) that kills competing models and unexpectedly leaves standing a new framework in which the universe begins as a finite, perfectly ordered “Pangaea object” of zero gravitational entropy that later breaks, generating time’s arrow, cosmic structure, and a thermodynamic map. Across nineteen “Pillars,” the book walks lay and expert readers through concrete calculations, spectral index without inflation, partial Hubble-tension relief, MOND-scale emergence, void kinematics, matter–antimatter asymmetry, and a de Sitter “Surface Death” end state, while narrating real-time arguments between AI systems like Grok and Claude over PASS versus NEAR-PASS results. In the final chapters, an axiomatic primitive “Axiom D” (distinction as the sole irreducible ingredient) is used to derive 3+1 dimensions, three fermion generations, and the world's first GR-compliant multiverse that falls out of the same algebra, tying cosmology to complexity, CRISPR biology, and the ethics of a universe that has begun to edit its own code. The past half-century in theoretical physics has witnessed a profound deviation from the discipline's foundational ethos: the relentless pursuit of empirically grounded, falsifiable explanations of nature. What began as a triumphant era, marked by the consolidation of the Standard Model of particle physics and the widespread acceptance of General Relativity, devolved into what can only be described as an extended orgy of intellectual folly, self-aggrandizement, and institutional capture by career incentives and funding imperatives. Consider the trajectory since the mid-1970s. The Standard Model, completed in its essential form by the early 1980s, accounted for all observed particles and interactions with extraordinary precision. Yet, rather than accepting this as a provisional but robust framework and directing resources toward its experimental refinement or toward unresolved tensions (such as quantum gravity or cosmological anomalies), the field embarked on a speculative proliferation unmatched in prior scientific epochs. String theory, supersymmetry, grand unified theories, eternal inflation with its multiverse landscape, loop quantum gravity, and myriad variants of quantum foundations emerged not as responses to acute empirical crises but as mathematically seductive extensions pursued for their internal elegance and the promise of unification at arbitrarily high energies. These frameworks share a common pathology: they have failed to yield a single verifiable prediction that has withstood experimental scrutiny. Over four decades, string theory has generated no testable low-energy signatures; supersymmetry has evaded detection at ever-higher collider energies; inflationary models have multiplied into an uncountable array of parameter-tuned variants, each retrofitted to accommodate cosmic microwave background observations without falsifiable novelty. The multiverse hypothesis, often invoked to explain fine-tuning, renders itself empirically sterile by construction, untestable in principle, it serves primarily as a philosophical escape hatch rather than a scientific advance. This stagnation stands in stark contrast to the rigorous demands of what might be termed the GR-Razor: a protocol insisting on General Relativity primacy, thermodynamic closure at every scale, ontological parsimony, and end-to-end predictive traceability from axiomatic foundations to observable consequences. Under such a criterion, mainstream paradigms reveal their deficiencies. ΛCDM cosmology, for instance, relies on ad hoc dark sectors, dark matter particles and a cosmological constant, neither derived from first principles nor integrated with gravitational dynamics in a thermodynamically consistent manner. The Horizon Problem, once cited as necessitating inflation, dissolves when one adopts a finite, non-singular initial state with inherent causal structure. The Hubble Tension, persistently misframed as a crisis requiring exotic modifications, reduces to geometric backreaction effects in an inhomogeneous, finite cosmology. These resolutions emerge not from parameter fitting but from enforcing structural necessity within Einstein's equations alone. The human dimension of this malaise is equally damning. Theoretical physics has increasingly rewarded those who produce voluminous publications, secure large grants, deliver polished conference addresses, and cultivate networks within elite institutions. Careers are built not on decisive empirical confrontation but on the perpetual deferral of testability: "just beyond the reach of the next accelerator" or "at Planck-scale energies forever inaccessible." Self-congratulation abounds in review articles and popular expositions that celebrate mathematical beauty as proxy for truth, while genuine progress, measurable by novel, confirmed predictions, remains absent. The field has become a closed ecosystem of mutual reinforcement, where criticism is marginalized as unconstructive or philosophically naive, and where funding flows to those who perpetuate the dominant narrative rather than challenge its foundational assumptions. This is not mere incremental slowdown; it is a systemic failure of scientific method. True theories, historically, achieve closure: they are constructed from minimal axioms, derive observables end-to-end, and submit to decisive experimental arbitration. General Relativity itself exemplifies this: proposed in 1915, it yielded immediate predictions (perihelion precession, light deflection) confirmed within years. Quantum electrodynamics followed suit, with precision tests at the level of ten decimal places. In contrast, the post-1970s speculative edifice has produced no analogous triumphs. Instead, it has accumulated epicycles, extra dimensions, branes, swampland conjectures, anthropic selection effects, each layer added to salvage prior commitments rather than to confront observational discord. The cost is not merely intellectual. Vast resources, human talent, computational infrastructure, public funding, have been diverted into pursuits that, under rigorous audit, fail the test of necessity. A reset is overdue: one that restores empiricism as sovereign, demands thermodynamic integrity, and enforces GR as the irreducible substrate of cosmology and gravity. Only by excising the accretions of unchecked speculation and careerist inertia can physics reclaim its mandate as a disciplined inquiry into the architecture of reality. The alternative is continued stagnation, where theories multiply without resolution, and the discipline risks descending into elegant but ultimately barren mathematics. This body of work declares that the future of cosmology no longer lies in speculative proliferation but in structural reduction. The GR-Razor and Cosmological Pangaea together define a successor architecture, thermodynamically grounded, geometrically inevitable, and ontologically complete. In this framework, existence is not a spectrum of possibilities but the single allowable configuration permitted by General Relativity and the second law. What this collectively represents is not a refinement of the standard model but a comprehensive reset: singularity removed, inflation displaced, dark matter reinterpreted, baryogenesis geometrized, multiverse bounded, dimensionality derived, particle generations explained, and thermodynamics made foundational rather than decorative.The age of describing what the universe might be has ended. The age of deriving what it must be begins here. This is the foundational axiom for cosmology’s succession: necessity, not speculation, is the prime law of creation. title: The Ancient Unconscious: Psychoanalysis and the Ancient Text by Vered Lev Kenaan
authors: Anne Mills
abstract: Reviewed by: The Ancient Unconscious: Psychoanalysis and the Ancient Text by Vered Lev Kenaan A.D. Mills (bio) The Ancient Unconscious: Psychoanalysis and the Ancient Text by Vered Lev Kenaan. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2019, 240 pages. Dream Time: The Poetics of Freudian Interpretation Late in The Ancient Unconscious (Kenaan, 2019), the classicist and comparatist Vered Lev Kenaan describes a genealogy for Freudian hermeneutics. Constituted on the strength of his acquaintance with the doctrine of typology, Freud's interpretative method preserves the distinction between the operative and the latent, the literal and the figural, devised by Early Christian exegetists to reconcile two sacred texts, temporally and theologically estranged: the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament.1 The Augustinian injunction to read beneath and against the Bible's literal import for its spiritual sense opened the text to a theological horizon that at once depended on and revealed its immanent tie to the New Testament. Thus, in the encounter between texts, Hosea or Jehoshua, leader of the Israelites after Moses, becomes a locus both of analepsis and prolepsis as an anticipation of Christ belatedly recovered. Coined by Tertullian, the textual principle of figura futurorum, a figure of things to come, is the name for this structure of vision whereby Hebraic persons and signs relate to those in Christianity "as umbrae, shadows, or imagines," shades obscuring and promising a richer meaning to be revealed only in the fullness of time (Kenaan, 2019, p. 155). Kenaan observes that, according to this temporally-organized method, "both the Old and the New Testaments are provisional and incomplete […] [t]his shared sense of incompleteness is what necessitates a process of interpretation binding the two together" (Kenaan, 2019, p. 157). [End Page 753] Psychoanalytic understanding seems profoundly informed by this textual practice: for Freud too, the past and the future create two temporal horizons, two unfinished texts, set apart but desirous of one another. Together, the analyst and analysand seek the mutually redemptive points of juncture whereby the future-present of the therapeutic encounter gains gravity from the past, while the past receives from this its future grace of significance. Figura futurorum, translated into the language of psychoanalysis, becomes Nachträglichkeit, afterwardness, or the deferral of meaning. Central to both biblical and psychoanalytic exegesis, then, is a handling of temporality whereby futural horizons contract and the past prolongs itself such that all time is never less than present: "In the unconscious nothing can be brought to an end, nothing is past or forgotten" (Freud, 1900, p. 577). Kenaan terms this heuristic "anachronic textuality," and it is, she suggests, in the manifestations of the Freudian unconscious that the power of a confusion of times to generate significance is most arrestingly evinced; anachronic textuality is "the domain of the unconscious" (Kenaan, 2019, p. 11). The exegetical temporality of psychoanalysis and the temporality of the unconscious itself are seen to coincide. For Kenaan, Freud's unconscious is chiefly a paradigm or organizational principle that brooks little respect for the linear, sequential time that the self relates to in conscious life. Handling memories, dreams, and fantasies with an esoteric grammar of condensation, displacement, free association, and symbolisation, the effect of the unconscious is a fusion of temporal perspectives, a way of being in time unlike any other the subject ordinarily inhabits. Although psychoanalysis and temporality is not a common topic among scholars and clinicians, thinking of the unconscious as a domain of temporal bricolage is fairly characteristic of what work there is on this subject. This is striking because it is seemingly so at odds with Freud's statements, which indicate the wholesale absence of temporal dynamics from unconscious activities. In the essay "The Unconscious," Freud writes that "the processes of the Ucs [unconscious] system are timeless; i.e. they are not ordered temporally, are not altered by the passage of time; they have no reference to time at all" (1915, p. 187). It seems that the "processes" Freud describes are unexpectedly fixed, pinioned to an atemporal or [End Page 754] "timeless" structure. title: European Medicines Agency seeks stakeholders' views on future transparency measures for clinical trials
authors: Rosa Gonzalez‐Quevedo; Laura Pioppo; Juan García Burgos; Peter R. Arlett
abstract: Academics, clinical researchers, drug developers and other key stakeholders such as patient advocates are being encouraged to take part in a public consultation1 recently launched by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) that will inform re-shaping of the EU transparency rules for clinical trials. Delivering high levels of transparency on clinical trials, including on clinical trial protocols and results, is one of the core aims of the Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) No. 536/2014 (CTR).2 The CTR introduces major changes in the way clinical trial applications are authorized in the EU/EEA, including harmonized requirements for clinical trial applications content, joint assessment carried out by the Member States as well as an increased level of transparency. On 31 January 2022, the Agency launched the Clinical Trials Information System (CTIS),3 as the IT platform enabling the implementation of the CTR and delivering clinical trials transparency that allows the public and researchers alike to access the clinical trials information. Based on the current transparency rules, CTIS includes a public database that enables the public to access information on the clinical trials registered in the system. This includes the main characteristics of the trial (design, scientific and, where applicable, therapeutic intent, title, identification of the investigational medicinal products [IMPs], treatment arms, treatment population and number of subjects, inclusion and exclusion criteria and main objectives and endpoints); member states where the trials will be running/recruiting; conclusion of the assessment and decision on the trial issued by the member states concerned; information updated during the trial to indicate the start and end dates of recruitment; substantial modifications to the trial, and the end date of the trial, with reasons for which trials are ended prematurely where it applies. In addition, 12 months after finalization of the clinical trial, a summary of the trial's results and a layman's summary, both prepared by the sponsor of the trial, will be made available through CTIS. CTIS will also include the clinical study reports (CSRs) for clinical trials conducted in the EU under the CTR, which are included as part of a marketing authorisation application. Sharing clinical trial data enables patients to enrol in clinical trials. It is also paramount for the clinical research community to identify the right clinical development pathway while avoiding unnecessary duplication of trials, providing a more efficient process that directs resources towards a more innovative pipeline. Moreover, when clinical trial data are open to public scrutiny, as constantly demanded by patients, consumers advocacy groups and the scientific community, a unique opportunity arises for ensuring that the public understands trial conduct, design and results, which helps to build public trust and understanding into how medicines are developed and researched. This can then be translated into the willingness of EU citizens to participate in clinical trials as an essential part of medical progress, and also reinforce public trust in clinical trial outcomes and the decisions taken by regulators based on such outcomes. Another important advantage is that registration of clinical trials in a public trials registry is a prerequisite for publication of the results in a peer reviewed journal,4 opening for further scrutiny of clinical trial data by the research community. In general, the level of protection provided by EU law to commercial confidential information aims at striking a balance between guaranteeing transparency on scientific information and allowing sponsors to get a return from their research and development efforts. In this context, EU law provides several incentives for investment in new medicines or new therapeutic uses of approved medicines. When publishing information related to clinical trials, it is necessary to avoid publishing personal data or commercially confidential information, in accordance with requirements laid down in the legislation and implementing guidelines. This may require certain commercially confidential information included in sponsors' applications, such as data on ongoing research and development, to be exempted from publication depending on the stage of development. The current transparency rules applying to CTIS are defined in the Appendix on disclosure rules,5 a document endorsed in 2015 by EMA's Management Board. This document was created by EMA during the development of CTIS, in consultation with the EU Member States and the European Commission. One of the key aspects of the current disclosure rules is the definition of clinical trials categories and corresponding deferral mechanisms, which allow trial sponsors to propose to delay the publication of some clinical trials documents, including protocols, which is then assessed by the Member States during the evaluation of the trial application. Some stakeholders have raised concerns on the deferrals timelines,6 specifically on the possibility of deferring publication of clinical trial protocols for phase II and phase III trials for up to 5 years after end of the trial in the EU/EEA. In that instance, publication of the protocol would de-facto occur after the publication of the summary of results that are published soon after submission in CTIS, due 12 months after the end of trial in the EU/EEA. Despite existing literature supporting that phase I trials pose generally a low risk of harm to participants, there have been some calls within the academic community to increase transparency on these early trials.7 In case of phase I trials, current rules in CTIS allow to defer the publication of clinical trials information for up to 7 years after the end of the trial in the EU/EEA for documents such as the clinical trial protocol, the safety and efficacy sections of the IMP dossier and investigator brochure. In addition, the results of either the interim analysis or the final analysis and layman's summary can be published up to 30 months after the end of the trial in the EU/EEA.5 It is important to note that balancing transparency with protection of commercial confidential information is particularly acute for the trials conducted with new investigational medicinal products, new pharmaceutical forms or routes of administration of already authorized products. The summary of results will also provide the public with valuable information about the trial design and its conduct, including aspects such as statistical analyses, inclusion–exclusion criteria, dosing regime, route and mode of administration and treatment period. The deferral is one of the key aspects of the present public consultation on which the Agency is seeking further input from users and stakeholders, in particular, whether redaction of documents could be a more balanced alternative to the deferral, resulting in earlier public access to the trial protocol/documents while still protecting CCI. It is important to add that for clinical trials used as part of a marketing authorisation application, the CSRs must be submitted to CTIS once a decision on the marketing authorisation has been issued or the application has been withdrawn. This CSR upload will automatically trigger the publication of all documents available in CTIS that supported the clinical development of the newly authorized medicine, including protocols, for any trial category regardless of whether the deferrals timelines had been reached. Importantly, for paediatric trials and for trials that are part of a paediatric investigational plan, all the key clinical trial information including documents (e.g., trial protocol) are published as soon as the decision on the clinical trial application is issued by the first Member State Concerned,4 therefore ensuring that ethical concerns regarding potential trial duplication in children are addressed. Achieving an adequate balance between transparency of trials and protection of confidentiality of proprietary data to maintain a healthy innovative pharmaceutical sector is a challenge. The ongoing public consultation is an opportunity for stakeholders, in particular academics and the clinical researchers, to voice their views. The public consultation intends to also collect views from system users and general clinical trial stakeholders on principles for simplification of existing rules. It requests responders to identify key elements submitted in a clinical trial application, and during the trial life cycle, considered critically important for early publication. The public consultation will be open until 28 June 2023 with feedback collected in an anonymized format. The result of the public consultation will inform changes in the EU public database (CTIS) to improve future users' experience and reduce the burden for sponsors while ensuring that the highest standards of transparency are met. The clinical trial landscape in the EU is adjusting to promote clinical research and innovation in an increasingly competitive environment. Clinical trials transformation is taking shape through the Accelerating Clinical Trials in the EU (ACT EU) initiative,8 and on the basis of the CTR. Transparency of EU clinical trials remains a priority9 for the EMRN in this context and the ongoing public consultation will help to ensure that stakeholders and citizens can shape it to best meet their needs. We thank Melanie Carr and Steffen Thirstrup for the review of the manuscript. The authors declare no competing interests. title: Heavy metals in red blood cells: From “Iron Maiden” to “Lead” Zeppelin
authors: Angelo D’Alessandro
abstract: Blood transfusion is a life-saving medical intervention, which makes packed red blood cells (RBCs) a life-saving drug. Unlike other drugs, whose chemical synthesis ensures standardization of the production process, RBCs are biological products that result from the essential, altruistic gift of tens of millions of donors around the world every year. As blood is stored under blood bank conditions, a series of biochemical and morphological changes occur – the so-called storage lesion(s)1—that have been posited to negatively impact the safety and efficacy of transfusion therapies,2-4 such as the capacity of stored RBCs to circulate5 or deliver oxygen6 after transfusion. As prospective randomized clinical trials have provided reassuring evidence about the non-inferiority of standard of practice versus the selective transfusion of the freshest available products,7 the focus of the transfusion research community has gradually shifted toward the appreciation of the impact of donor biology and genetic factors on the onset, progression, and, ultimately, severity of the so-called storage lesion.8, 9 Informed by the convergent interpretation of population studies on ex vivo and in vivo hemolysis both in humans10, 11 and rodent models of storage and transfusion,12 a new paradigm has evolved to reevaluate the storage lesion in light of the role of factors such as processing (additive solutions, plasticizers, irradiation, and pathogen reduction) and donor biology (age, sex, ethnicity, and body mass index)—as well as donor diet or other exposures (e.g., smoking, alcohol consumption, and drugs that are not grounds for blood donor deferral).13-19 Since what is in a blood unit ends up in the circulatory system of a recipient, certain donor exposures are of special relevance to certain categories of vulnerable recipients, especially pediatric recipients who rely on massive transfusion as part of invasive surgical procedures (e.g., cardiopulmonary bypass) or life-long transfusions secondary to hematological disorders (e.g., sickle cell disease). Such exposures include factors such as plasticizers that leach from the blood bag,20 all the way to "forever chemicals" such as perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), whose accumulation in the bloodstream is exacerbated in some volunteer donors owing to professional exposures (e.g., firemen).21 Historically, heavy metal metabolism in RBCs has almost exclusively focused on iron, owing to the essential role of this element in hemoglobin synthesis and oxygen transport (2.6 g, 66% of bodily iron is in RBCs22). However, other heavy metals warrant further investigation in RBCs, not just from a basic science standpoint, but also from a translational, transfusion medicine-centered perspective. Indeed, in this issue of TRANSFUSION, Hadjesfandiari et al. from the Devine lab report the results from an impressive study entitled, "Measurement of Lead, Mercury, and Cadmium in Blood Donors in Canada". The investigators conducted an impressive and comprehensive analysis of these heavy metals across 2529 Canadian blood donors to assess potential risk associated with transfusions, particularly in neonates. Utilizing inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, the team aimed to identify the prevalence of these metals above the recommended safety thresholds for neonatal transfusion, with reportedly 2.2% and 0.4% of donations testing above such thresholds for lead or mercury, respectively. Cadmium was present at generally lower levels, though was still of concern. The study revealed significant correlations between higher metal levels and older donor age, emphasizing the need for targeted blood selection in transfusions, especially for vulnerable groups. Sex dimorphism was also observed, with higher levels of lead in male donors and cadmium in females. Geographical variations were also notable; clinics near industrial sites or mines showed elevated metal concentrations, suggesting local environmental factors as significant contributors to these levels. This study underscores the necessity of integrating donor demographic and geographic data in transfusion management practices to minimize potential risks from heavy metal exposure. Overall, it supports a strategic approach in the selection and use of blood units, potentially guiding policy enhancements to ensure the safety of blood transfusions, particularly for at-risk populations like neonates. Since heavy metals accumulate in blood over time, life-long exposures compound to potentially accrue above safety thresholds for pediatric recipients, posing concerns about the need to screen for these compounds at donation to mitigate potential risk increase when transfusing blood from older donors into pediatric recipients. As the median age of the blood donor population is increasing worldwide, while recruitment of younger donors has slowed down over the past decades, especially after the COVID-19 pandemic, the work by Hadjesfandiari and colleagues raises important questions that warrant further evaluation as to whether novel transfusion guidelines should consider heavy metals or associated biological (age, sex) or geographical factors in the near future, at least in the management of pediatric transfusion. A diametrically reversed perspective that this study offers pertains to the focus on the donor population. Ultra-high-throughput technology is now available to offer at scale, free to the donor and with theoretically negligible cost/unit for blood services, the molecular characterization of donated blood at the genomic and small molecule level. The latter testing could include heavy metals, but also a full metabolic and exposome panel, beyond what is currently offered in state-of-the-art standard clinical chemistry metabolic panel assays. The implementation of these approaches at scale may not only represent a unique recruitment and retention strategy, while also offering an epidemiological window on some of the healthiest subjects in any given population, blood donors, but may also and foremost represent a token of gratitude toward the millions of self-less volunteers who donate hope without asking anything in exchange. The title of this editorial is a cheesy pun on heavy metals in blood, inspired by the role of iron in erythrocyte biology, historically regarded as mere iron carriers, and by the names of two the most iconic all time "heavy metal" rock bands, Iron Maiden, and Led Zeppelin. title: Protected Quantum Observable Readout for Hybrid Workflows: A Refresh Primitive on IBM Kingston Heron r3 Quantum Processor [Correction appended July 2026: mechanism reinterpretation — operational results retained]
authors: Amit Brahmbhatt

abstract: CORRECTION NOTICE (July 2026) — Mechanism Reinterpretation. Operational Results Retained. Subsequent algebraic analysis and additional hardware sessions (IBM Kingston, July 2026) require a correction to the interpretive framing of this record. All measured data, job identifiers, and the operational refresh result reported below are retained unchanged. What is retained. All hardware measurements and statistics as published, including the delay-sweep values for all four conditions. The operational finding: a midpoint refresh operation extends the actionable window of the measured observable beyond the point at which both passive strategies fail. This result has since been independently reproduced in a July 2026 session on the same device. The hybrid decision-workflow framing (actionability thresholds; abstention below threshold). What is superseded. The passive-protection interpretation. This record framed the Y⊗Z construction as a "protected plane" providing geometric coherence protection. Subsequent analysis shows the measured observable factorizes exactly into a product of single-qubit expectation values, with zero connected correlation. No entangled protected subspace is present in the preparation, and the construction does not satisfy the invariance conditions required for a passive decoherence-free subspace (dominant local error generators act non-trivially within the proposed eigenspace). The explanation offered for the C3 (protected hold) result. The original text attributed C3's underperformance to gate overhead while stating it "does not invalidate the protection claim." The corrected interpretation is simpler: there is no passive protection mechanism. An observable oriented orthogonally to the dephasing axis is maximally exposed to dephasing, not shielded from it; C3's behavior is the expected physics. The mechanism attributed to C4 (refresh). Refresh works because midpoint re-preparation halves the free-evolution exposure of the signal, which quantitatively predicts the observed window extension. The benefit is delivered by the refresh operation and is independent of the specific operator orientation. The phrase "the protective geometry is still useful when combined with refresh" is withdrawn. Forward-looking claims regarding "a new class of computational advantage" arising from a "specific geometric subspace where structured information survives longer" are withdrawn. Corrected statement of the record's contribution. On IBM Kingston, a midpoint refresh primitive extended the actionable window of a measured observable inside a threshold-gated hybrid decision workflow, where passive strategies failed earlier. The mechanism is active re-preparation (exposure halving), not passive subspace protection. The workflow machinery — per-condition actionability verdicts and abstention below threshold — stands as published. Relationship to prior records. We prepared the Y⊗Z stabilizer state on IBM Kingston using the same four-qubit module [13, 14, 15, 19] validated in prior QuantaCore campaigns, inserted variable delays from 0 to 25 microseconds, and measured the primary stabilizer observable |YZII| under four conditions. We defined an actionability threshold of |YZII| > 0.5 — the signal level above which a classical controller can reliably distinguish the structured observable from noise and act on it. The result is clear and operationally meaningful. Passive delayed readout becomes non-actionable by 15 microseconds (|YZII| = 0.479, below threshold). Passive protected hold degrades similarly, also falling below threshold at 15 microseconds (|YZII| = 0.314). By contrast, refresh-cadenced re-injection of the protected state — resetting all qubits at the midpoint and re-preparing the full Y⊗Z stabilizer — remains actionable at 15 microseconds (|YZII| = 0.611, above threshold). At 25 microseconds, all delayed conditions fall below threshold. Why this matters: This experiment bridges the physical characterisation of prior records into an operational hybrid-workflow context. The question is no longer "how long does the protected state survive?" but "how long can a controller use it?" The answer, on current Kingston hardware, is: passive readout and passive hold lose actionability by 15 microseconds, while refresh-cadenced re-injection extends actionability to at least 15 microseconds. This identifies refresh as the operationally viable strategy for hybrid workflows requiring structured observable access beyond the passive coherence window. More broadly, this result points toward a new class of computational advantage available on NISQ-era hardware — not by running longer or deeper circuits, but by actively managing the structured quantum signal that fragile computations depend on. Current NISQ devices are noisy, short-lived, and error-prone, which makes most quantum algorithms impractical at scale. But the Y⊗Z protected plane offers a different path: rather than fighting decoherence globally, it identifies a specific geometric subspace where structured information survives longer, and pairs it with a refresh protocol that periodically re-injects that structure before it degrades below usefulness. This is not quantum error correction in the fault-tolerant sense — it makes no claim to preserving arbitrary logical content indefinitely. What it does offer is something more immediately practical: a protected observable primitive that keeps a fragile structured signal actionable long enough for a classical controller to use it. On hardware where unprotected signals routinely wash out before the control loop can respond, that is a meaningful and demonstrable advantage. It suggests that hybrid quantum-classical workflows on near-term devices can be made more reliable not by waiting for better hardware, but by choosing the right geometric subspace, the right observable, and the right refresh cadence for the task at hand. The experiment uses the proven 12-gate Y⊗Z stabilizer preparation from prior QuantaCore records and sweeps five delay times (0, 5, 10, 15, 25 microseconds) under four conditions, measuring the primary stabilizer observable YZII as the structured signal available to a classical controller. Four conditions were tested: C1 (Immediate reference): Y⊗Z state prepared and measured without delay. Establishes full-strength baseline. Stable at |YZII| ≈ 0.68 across all delay points, confirming coherent observable mapping throughout the experiment. C2 (Passive delayed readout): Y⊗Z state prepared, delay inserted, measured. No protection protocol during delay. Decays from 0.665 at tau = 0 to 0.479 at tau = 15 microseconds (below threshold) and 0.342 at tau = 25 microseconds. C3 (Protected hold): Y⊗Z state prepared, delay inserted, measured. The Y⊗Z geometry provides passive coherence protection during the delay. Decays from 0.670 at tau = 0 to 0.314 at tau = 15 microseconds (below threshold) and 0.074 at tau = 25 microseconds. Underperforms passive delayed readout at late times, consistent with gate overhead interacting with decoherence. C4 (Protected refresh): Y⊗Z state prepared, delay tau/2 inserted, all qubits reset and full Y⊗Z state re-prepared, delay tau/2 inserted, measured. Decays from 0.680 at tau = 0 to 0.611 at tau = 15 microseconds (above threshold) and 0.374 at tau = 25 microseconds. Actionability threshold: |YZII| > 0.5 — defined as the signal level at which a classical controller can distinguish the structured observable from noise with confidence sufficient to gate a workflow action. Key result: At tau = 15 microseconds, C2 and C3 are both non-actionable (✗), while C4 alone remains actionable (✓). This is the first demonstration in the QuantaCore program of a concrete hybrid-workflow criterion — controller actionability — that distinguishes refresh-cadenced re-injection from both passive delayed readout and passive protected hold.
