title: Impasses of the Nation: The Practical Political Philosophy of Marcel Mauss
authors: Rosalind C. Morris
abstract: The nation is an enigmatic phenomenon, explains Marcel Mauss in his draft notes for the never-completed book, La Nation.1 It is a rare and recently emergent political form, he asserts, but it is preceded by the experience of nationality and the practices of international— or, as he prefers to term them, intersocial (and perhaps more properly named intersocietal) relations. It is a medium for administering a nationalized economy but something other than the state. It is a product of integration, but it is also defined by a tendency to individuation, separation, and even isolation. It is characterized by the recession of intermediary political institutions such as the clan and the tribe, but also by the generalization of an increasingly totalizing technical mediation, one that exceeds the nation while conditioning its possibility. As a corollary, the nation is a form in which individuals are linked to each other as subjects in an apparently immediate relation to a self-consciously apprehended object. It is also distinguished by a tendency among its members to mischaracterize as origin what is co-emergent with its own appearance. It is an agency of warfare and the medium of its suspension. It is more than an ethnos, other than the state, at once emergent and still to come.The objective historical contradictions of the nation proliferate in seeming proportion to its function as regulative ideal. Such is the enigma of the nation for Marcel Mauss. That the book in which these propositions were made was never completed may be a result of the impasses to which his reflections repeatedly led, and which, in the end, he could only resolve in a displaced mode, by an analysis not of the modern nation but of the “archaic” institution of the gift. The impasses were also practical and political, and they can be understood in terms of the context in which he wrote: the immediate post-World War I era, in which the attempt to generate an apparatus of international peace and reconciliation—via reparations and principles administered by international legal institutions—floundered as working-class nationalism and cosmopolitan capitalism allied against the more equitable ambitions of the radical socialist and cooperativist movements to which Mauss was himself deeply committed. In the opening (and earliest written) sections of La Nation, Mauss outlines his project in relatively simple terms. He commences by acknowledging that the problems of individualism and the antinomy between the nation and the state have been well analyzed by political theorists, and practically resolved in the overthrow of tyrannies and the establishment of civil society. This leaves the matter of relations between antagonistic groups within and among nations, the analysis of which Mauss hoped could enable an avoidance of war and especially of the total sort exemplified by World War I. Finally, there is the aspiration to realize the potential of the nation, in particular the French nation. Here, Mauss proposes to consider socializing and nationalizing tendencies through which nations could become in practice what they are in ideality: “masters of their economy” comprised of “natural title: In Search of Bunny Burgess, or Down the Rabbit Hole: Anecdotes, Secret Histories, and The Great Gatsby
authors: Sarah Churchwell
abstract: Anecdote: Something yet unpublished; secret history. – Samuel Johnson, A Dictionary of the English Language WhenThe Great Gatsbywaspublished in 1925, H. L. Mencken famously declared that it was ‘in form no more than a glorified anecdote’.1 This story is obviously unimportant … What ails it, fundamentally, is the plain fact that it is simply a story. … The story, for all its basic triviality, has a fine texture, a careful and brilliant finish. … ‘The Great Gatsby’, [is] a far inferior story at bottom … Fitzgerald, the stylist, arises to challenge Fitzgerald, the social historian, but I doubt that the latter ever quite succumbs to the former. The thing that chiefly interests the basic Fitzgerald is still the florid show of modern American life – and especially the devil’s dance that goes on at the top. … Their idiotic pursuit of sensation, their almost incredible stupidity and triviality, their glittering swinishness – these are the things that go into his notebook.2 What makes Gatsby an anecdote, for Mencken, is that it is ‘simply a story’, a ‘story [that] is obviously unimportant’, a story of ‘basic triviality’, ‘a far inferior story’. This repetitive assertion is not a definition, of course, but a tautology. The charge of anecdotalism also implicitly relates, for Mencken, to the novel’s function as social history, a contemporary record of ‘the devil’s dance’ of the jazz-age rich on Long Island. The triviality of the (real) people being evoked converges in Mencken’s judgement with the triviality of the story depicting them. He does not mention the novel’s brevity, only what he sees as its flimsiness: this is what makes it no more than an anecdote. But Mencken also suggests that its anecdotalism bears a tacit relation to notebooks, although whether he is calling Gatsby itself a notebook or merely supposing that it transcribes Fitzgerald’s own notebook documenting what he saw around him is unclear. Either way, the charge of anecdotalism is related to the idea of reportage, to a cultural hierarchy that values (what it recognises as legitimate) aesthetic forms over historiographical notebooks. The anecdote sits uncertainly somewhere between gossip and story, between history and art, its potential for meaning still contested. The question of what exactly distinguishes an anecdote from a story ‘proper’ remains an open one, with definitions tending to conflate qualitative and quantitative distinctions, so that an anecdote’s brevity is related to its insubstantiality, but also to its lack of immanent or transferable meaning.3 For Dr Johnson, an anecdote was first something ‘yet unpublished’, and second a ‘secret history’. The OED gives priority to this meaning (‘1. pl. Secret, private, or hitherto unpublished narratives or details of history’) before offering a more familiar definition: ‘2.a. The narrative of a detached incident, or of a single event, told as being in itself interesting or striking. (At first, an item of gossip.)’ Detachment as discontinuity is what differentiates the anecdote from other types of storytelling: the more attached or continuous it becomes, the less it is anecdotal. Anecdotalism is thus relative, not categorical; and its history associates it with gossip. This essay follows the trail of an anecdote that intersects with the formation of The Great Gatsby, the (re)construction of which may provide some insight into the role gossip and anecdote played in that formation. The story here traced is an anecdote in the Johnsonian sense of an unpublished, secret history, a hunt for a forgotten story to which Fitzgerald returned again and again in his memories of the production of Gatsby, an anecdote that refers to a man called Bunny Burgess. Pursuing the traces of this lost anecdote creates a trail that shows where problems of form converge with problems of intention, which is also where the textual comes up against the biographical. In the case of a novel like Gatsby, pursuing an anecdote associated with its origins invokes not only its social-historical meanings, but also its formal choices: brevity as a conscious withholding, resistance to epistemological certainty, elusiveness and fragmentation, refusal of plenitude, and deferral of meaning. Fitzgerald wrote to Mencken the day after his review appeared, explicitly defending his novel’s form against charges of anecdotalism: ‘the influence on [Gatsby] has been the masculine one of The Brothers Karamazov, a thing of incomparable form, rather than the feminine one of The Portrait of a Lady. If it seems trivial or “anecdotal” it is because of an aesthetic fault, a failure in one very important episode and not a frailty in the theme’.4 Having invoked the strong ‘masculinity’ of a fictive work of ‘incomparable form’ to defend his novel against charges of anecdotal ‘frailty’, Fitzgerald went on to write a much more exasperated letter to his friend Edmund Wilson, also invoking Karamazov to complain that no one, including Mencken, understood the actual meanings of Gatsby: Without making any invidious comparisons between Class A and Class C, if my novel is an anecdote so is The Brothers Karamazov. From one angle the latter could be reduced into a detective story. … Of all the reviews, even the most enthusiastic, not one had the slightest idea what the book was about.5 For Fitzgerald, the difference between art and anecdote is qualitative: if his novel seemed trivial, it was because of an aesthetic failure, not because its theme was ‘frail’. title: News and Community Behind Barbed Wire: The Topaz Times and Japanese American Incarceration in Utah
authors: Glen Feighery
abstract: On a Thursday in March 1943, Masaomi Yano sat at a table, head bowed as he made a stencil for a mimeograph machine. The twenty-five-year-old California native was translating English-language articles into Japanese for the bilingual newspaper he worked for. Like a typical small-town paper, it included items about a new golf course, sewing classes, and a bridge tournament, as well as a funeral announcement. The newspaper's readers didn't live in a typical community, however. They were confined at the Central Utah Relocation Project, better known as the Topaz internment (incarceration) camp, during World War II.Topaz was one of ten such camps, with others in California, Arizona, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and Arkansas. They held 120,000 people of Japanese descent who had been removed from the West Coast after the attack on Pearl Harbor. Facing political and military pressure, President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, authorizing the mass evacuation of people—two-thirds of them US citizens—who had violated no laws. Between March and May 1942, Japanese immigrants (Issei) and second-generation Japanese Americans (Nisei) were forced from their homes and placed in crude temporary “assembly centers,” often fairgrounds or racetracks. Between May and October 1942, evacuees were moved to the ten semi-permanent relocation camps, where most remained throughout the war.1The Topaz camp occupied one square mile in the Sevier Desert of Millard County, sixteen miles northwest of Delta, near the tiny settlement of Abraham.2 Topaz was divided into dozens of blocks with military-style barracks, latrines, mess halls, and laundries. Living accommodations were spartan: Each barrack was divided into small “apartments,” bare rooms with a window, wood stove, and light bulb suspended from the ceiling. At its peak, the camp held 8,130 people, who worked as cooks, teachers, nurses, and firefighters and did most other jobs of running the community. People also attended church, played in sports leagues, gave music recitals, and read their local newspaper, the Topaz Times. This population was Utah's fifth-largest city at the time, a city behind barbed wire and watched by Army guards.3At the eightieth anniversary of Topaz's closure, this essay focuses on the intersection of Utah history and journalism history. It shows that Topaz functioned as a community in part because of the Topaz Times. Journalism historian David Paul Nord, who studied the connections between newspapers and the people they served, defined community as “common experience and sympathy, and a deep sense of interdependence,” as well as an “organized, common frame of reference” so people could “share a vision of social reality.”4 Newspapers accomplished this in two ways, Nord believed. They provided information to establish an “authority of facts” and served as a forum for debate and civic participation.5 Debate implied disagreement, which Nord portrayed as a hallmark of American democracy, because “to argue about the state was to be a member of the nation.”6This essay examines how the Times reported and commented on five episodes: setting up camp, the so-called loyalty oath, the killing of a resident by a guard, the military draft, and closing the camp. Through its coverage, the paper helped readers to identify as members of a discrete community, not just people thrown together by circumstance. It provided information, reflected Topaz's variety of voices, and bore witness to trauma. Also, as a Utah newspaper that published 438 issues between September 17, 1942, and August 31, 1945, the Times is worth consideration in its own right as a noteworthy publication in the history of the state.7In telling this history, it is important to consider language. Historian Roger Daniels objected to terms such as “internment” and “relocation,” calling them government euphemisms intended to obscure the lack of legal process. He noted that “incarcerated people themselves sometimes used the term concentration camp while they were in confinement.” Others agreed.8 Author Yoshiko Uchida concluded that “the ‘relocation centers’ are properly called concentration camps. The term is used not to imply any similarity to the Nazi death camps, but to indicate [their] true nature.”9 Utah historian Sandra C. Taylor argued that Topaz was “an armed concentration camp,” or at best, “a concentration camp with a human face.”10 However, many historians have adopted terms closer to those employed by the National Park Service and the Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians, using words such as “incarceration” and “prison camp” synonymously with “internment” and “relocation camp.”11 This essay follows a similar practice.Japanese American internment has been the subject of vast study. Daniels was the preeminent historian, portraying relocation as the result of racism and virulent nationalism fueled by resentment of Japanese Americans’ economic success. Like the other camps, Topaz was constructed in a remote location “where no one had lived before and no one has lived since,” Daniels observed. “The barbed-wire fences, the guards, and the surrounding wasteland were always there to remind the detainees that they were exiled, incarcerated Americans.”12 Authors Audrie Girdner and Anne Loftis also emphasized racial motivations. “In the West Coast hysteria that led to the evacuation, the Japanese, both aliens and citizens, were lumped together in a general racial indictment.”13 As will be seen, citizenship figured prominently in events the Topaz Times covered.Numerous historians have documented internment in Utah, beginning with Leonard J. Arrington. His comprehensive overview mentioned the harshness of the Topaz site, especially “the wind” and “seldom interrupted whirl of dust,” which turned to “gummy muck” after rain or snow. Arrington portrayed the Topaz Times as integral to community life, as it was “produced by evacuee staffs with a minimum of supervision and no overt exercise of censorship.”14 Uchida, who was incarcerated at Topaz with her parents and sister, described “an artificial government-spawned community on the periphery of the real world.” The alkaline dust was daunting, and she did not appreciate a Times item that told new arrivals they were “Residents, not Evacuees,” who should adopt a healthy “Mental Climate”—exhortations she found “patronizing.”15 A history of Millard County also dubbed Topaz an “artificial community” and remarked that Army recruitment was a “cause of serious unrest among the evacuees.”16 Allan Kent Powell situated Topaz in the context of Utah's role during World War II. The state was critical strategically and logistically, and importing more than eight thousand Japanese Americans added to racial tensions.17Taylor, a University of Utah historian, depicted the makeshift conditions, including that the camp was unfinished as people arrived. Built from pine boards and tar paper, structures had no insulation and “some barracks even lacked roofs,” she noted. Most people at Topaz were from Northern California, and “to people whose homes had been in the moist, green Bay Area, central Utah was a shock,” Taylor wrote.18 Social relations were also disrupted. “The breakdown in family life and the virtual disappearance of the individual home was devastating to women,” she found.19 As people were released, those settling in Utah were often unwelcome, even though the state lay well outside the West Coast exclusion zone.20 Taylor constructed her narratives from the extensive archives of the War Relocation Authority (WRA), oral history interviews with former residents, and issues of the Topaz Times. Taylor was somewhat dubious of the Times, asserting that it “cheerfully recorded” routine events but lacked a strong editorial voice. Still, she said, the newspaper was an “important institution in camp.”21Historians Linda L. Ivey and Kevin W. Kaatz also found that the Topaz Times was important to community life. News articles “detailed housing issues . . . and noted that it was particularly difficult to provide shelter and bedding for the new arrivals.”22 Topaz Museum founder Jane Beckwith explained the connections between Delta and Topaz. Her grandfather Frank A. Beckwith had close ties to the camp. He contributed articles to the Topaz literary journal TREK, and he hosted visiting Topaz Times staffers at the Millard County Chronicle. Beckwith's father hired a young man from the camp to help produce the Chronicle, which often reprinted news from the Times.23Topaz is often mentioned in internment histories because of the prominent people who were there, and curator Kenneth Hartvigsen chronicled the work of perhaps the most famous, artist Miné Okubo. Drawing from her 1946 graphic memoir Citizen 13660, Hartvigsen explored how Okubo used her art to “create a sense of control through creative action.” Internment was a “complicated and sometimes contradictory reality,” and she responded with “a truly radical text” that explored “the complex experience of trauma.”24 Okubo also created illustrations for the Topaz Times during its early life.25Much of the historical record about Topaz has been preserved in personal memoirs, oral histories, and the WRA archives. The Topaz Times is another primary source, often incorporated into secondary research. Histories of camp journalism have emphasized the lack of press freedom because the papers were published under WRA control.26 The most prolific scholar of camp newspapers, Takeya Mizuno, concluded
